articles.title: India needs its own AI safety framework, not a copy of US pact: Industry experts
articles.text:
India needs its own AI safety framework, not a copy of US pact: Industry experts
Under the accord, the companies committed to internal controls to monitor their AI models, dedicated oversight teams, independent external audits and board-level oversight.
India should build its own artificial intelligence (AI) safety framework suited to its languages, scale, and application-led AI ecosystem rather than replicate a voluntary pact signed by US President Donald Trump and top technology firms last week, industry experts said.
They also called for a commitment that brings together all stakeholders and tackles risks such as deepfakes and cyberattacks, even as they differed on whether voluntary measures alone would be enough.
The comments came after the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a voluntary AI safety pact signed on September 29 by Trump and top executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Nvidia and Elon Musk's xAI.
Under the accord, the companies committed to internal controls to monitor their AI models, dedicated oversight teams, independent external audits and board-level oversight. They also agreed to meet regularly to set safety standards.
Nasscom Chairman and Fractal Group CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said India should not simply replicate the US. Instead, it should use a domestic commitment as a building block towards a global understanding of AI safety.
"As models become more capable and agentic, we are giving them greater access to systems and greater autonomy to make decisions. AI safety must be strengthened considerably and must stay ahead of capability to prevent catastrophic risks," Velamakanni said.
He noted that the US accord is largely a push for self-policing by frontier AI companies. The European Union, by contrast, has taken a binding, risk-based approach, while China follows a state-directed control model.
India, the Nasscom Chairman said, could use its role in the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) and the momentum from hosting the AI Impact Summit in February to prevent worst-case outcomes, without citizens of India and the Global South being denied access to frontier models.
"India doesn't need to copy the US model, but it can take inspiration from it and expedite efforts to build a trusted AI ecosystem," said Soumen Mandal, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research.
He added that such a commitment should cover testing AI systems before deployment, independent audits, reporting serious problems, and naming people responsible for AI-related risks.
Amit Khanna, Partner and Automation Ecosystem Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat, said any commitment should be suited to Indian market conditions.
He noted that India's focus is on building AI applications rather than major foundational models.
"An industry commitment in India should ensure AI works reliably across vernacular languages and unique cultural contexts and should not exploit AI knowledge asymmetry in the population," Khanna said.
Ganesh Gopalan, co-founder and CEO of Gnani.ai, said any framework must ensure a level playing field.
Global frontier models should be subject to the same rules as Indian ones, he said, since Indian AI companies compete with global firms for the same customers.
The experts differed on whether self-regulation would be enough.
"Voluntary, self-regulatory approaches are necessary but woefully insufficient," Velamakanni said.
"Pharmaceuticals and aviation are great examples of industries where strong, technically competent regulators have strengthened safety and public trust without stopping innovation."
He said India needs binding rules on transparency, incident reporting, and accountability when serious harm occurs.
The IndiaAI Safety Institute should be strengthened to test newly released models, but without creating a bottleneck by requiring pre-release certification of every model, he added.
Mandal backed a hybrid approach. Mandatory rules would apply to potential harms in defence, healthcare, banking, and government use cases, while voluntary standards would cover fast-moving technical areas where regulators may lack technical expertise.
"This type of hybrid approach will provide flexibility to AI companies instead of restricting every line of code while ensuring safety and privacy are not compromised," he said.
Khanna also called for a hybrid "techno-legal" approach. It would pair a strong voluntary layer with binding mandates, such as the provisions on synthetically generated information in the IT Amendment Rules, 2026.
He said voluntary compliance alone leaves significant gaps, particularly in civil rights and public safety.
Gopalan, however, favoured self-regulation.
"Voluntary self-regulation is key given the technology is new. Having mandatory regulation can stifle competition and lead to concerns about a few companies getting preferential treatment.
"India needs more than 100 frontier AI lab companies, and that's the need of the hour to prevent India from being colonised, which is inevitable if we lag behind in the AI race," Gopalan said.
The Indian government is in the process of bringing in its own AI regulation. Earlier this year, IT Secretary S Krishnan noted that while existing legal provisions have so far been adequate in addressing initial concerns on issues like deepfakes and AI-generated synthetic content, an "additional regulation or law may be needed".
"It is a conversation which has commenced, and my minister (IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw) and I have both been on record earlier that we will look at AI regulation when the time is right, and it appears that the time is getting right, and we will start looking at it," he had said.
Vaishnaw had also said that the current information technology law was framed much before the rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and that a new legal framework may be required to deal with the changing landscape.
The industry agrees that any pact should go beyond AI companies.
"This cannot be an agreement among AI companies alone," Velamakanni said.
He said the government, frontier model developers, large deployers, including enterprises and public agencies, academia, and independent safety researchers should all have defined roles. Workers, users, and civil society should have formal channels to report harms.
He added that safety evaluations of frontier models should be carried out by independent, expert institutions and published, with narrow exceptions where disclosure itself creates a security risk.
Mandal said the agreement should bring together the entire AI ecosystem, from AI companies and their business users to regulators, universities, researchers, workers, and users.
Khanna argued that it should include government and public sector bodies, which would be major users of AI, as well as civil society, worker unions, and technology companies.
Meanwhile, Gopalan called for broader self-regulation across the AI ecosystem to ensure impartial access to limited compute resources.
Velamakanni said the top concern must be preventing catastrophic and systemic harms.
He listed large-scale cyberattacks, electoral interference, biological or chemical weapons, attacks on critical infrastructure, and loss of control over highly autonomous systems. Individual harms such as deepfakes, fraud, impersonation, privacy breaches, and self-harm come next.
"Autonomy must lag behind assurance to provide a margin of safety. As AI systems gain the ability to act in the world (use tools, move money, change systems, make consequential decisions), the evidence that they are safe and controllable must grow faster than the autonomy we give them," he said.
Gopalan said that given India's large population and democratic framework, the bigger concerns are deepfakes and cyberattacks targeting financial institutions.
Khanna also named deepfakes as the top immediate priority.
He described misinformation, deepfakes, and political manipulation as "existential threats to India's social fabric".
He said rules on liability when AI systems fail, such as misdiagnosing a patient or wrongly denying welfare benefits, remain a critical gap.
Mandal placed independent audits first, followed by accountability, data protection, deepfakes, and job impact.
"Without independent testing and audits, the system will not be complete, as companies may sometimes overlook AI-related concerns," he said.

articles.title: Un membre présumé de ShinyHunters arrêté en Jordanie aide le FBI
articles.text:
Arrêté le 29 septembre par les autorités jordaniennes, Saif al-Din Khader aide aujourd’hui le FBI à retrouver les autres membres de ShinyHunters. Il y a quelques jours, ce groupe d’extorsion a revendiqué le vol des données de l’ensemble des employés du bureau fédéral, dossiers médicaux et psychiatriques compris.
Trois personnes au fait du dossier ont confirmé cette arrestation à Reuters hier, sans préciser où le jeune homme est détenu. D’après deux d’entre elles, Saif al-Din Khader coopère avec le FBI, et il a guidé les enquêteurs dans ses appareils électroniques et ses correspondances numériques pour remonter jusqu’à ses complices.
Les pirates disent être entrés dans le portail de recrutement du bureau en contournant le pare-feu installé devant son serveur Oracle PeopleSoft. D'après l’échantillon analysé par l’agence de presse, les fichiers volés contiennent des informations médicales et psychiatriques sur les agents et des précisions sensibles sur les fonctions de certains employés.
Les enquêteurs du FBI peuvent désormais compter sur Saif al-Din Khader pour limiter les dégâts, ou du moins les comprendre, alors que les membres de ShinyHunters leur échappent depuis des années.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
Deux arrestations en deux semaines chez ShinyHunters
Avant l’interpellation de Saif al-Din Khader, la police néerlandaise a arrêté à Amsterdam, le 15 septembre, un homme de 24 ans dans le cadre d’une enquête sur ShinyHunters. Il s’agit de Pepijn van der Stap, d’après le journaliste Brian Krebs et le site DataBreaches. Sept jours plus tard, le groupe a revendiqué l'intrusion dans les systèmes du FBI, avec 2 à 3 To de données volées à la clé. Pour ShinyHunters, ce piratage était une riposte à un avis du FBI. Dans ce texte, le bureau accusait le groupe d’exagérer ses accès pour extorquer de l’argent à ses victimes, et les pirates lui ont laissé une semaine pour le retirer.
Après l’arrestation aux Pays-Bas, Brett Leatherman, directeur adjoint de la division cyber du FBI, a sommé les autres membres du groupe de se rendre. « Plus vous restez ici, plus nous en apprenons sur vous. Je vous suggère de prendre contact en premier, tant que vous avez encore le choix », a-t-il averti.
Mardi 29 septembre, jour où Saif al-Din Khader aurait été placé en détention, un affilié présumé de ShinyHunters a fermé son compte de messagerie, et le principal porte-parole du groupe a cessé de répondre aux journalistes de Reuters et de BleepingComputer. Le lendemain, le site du groupe sur le dark web a été mis hors ligne, et Kash Patel, directeur du FBI, a écrit sur X que « d’autres arrestations sont possibles ».
Interrogé, le bureau a refusé d’évoquer une arrestation précise, mais il a promis de « n’épargner aucun moyen pour traduire en justice chacun des responsables ». Dans leur dernier courriel à Reuters, les opérateurs de ShinyHunters ont adopté un ton conciliant. « Nous ne souhaitons pas d’escalade », ont-ils écrit, en ajoutant que l’agence pouvait comprendre que « ShinyHunters renonce complètement ». Jeudi 1er octobre, un nouveau site de fuite de données a cependant été mis en ligne au nom du groupe, et d’autres membres continuent donc probablement l’extorsion, d'après BleepingComputer.
Saif al-Din Khader, un pirate repéré depuis 2025
Saif al-Din Khader est lié à plusieurs fuites de données depuis début 2025. En février de cette année-là, il a diffusé 6,5 Go de documents volés à la filiale roumaine d’Orange. À l’époque, il appartenait au groupe de rançongiciel HellCat, mais il a affirmé à BleepingComputer avoir mené cette attaque seul. Le pirate a ensuite obtenu des droits d’administrateur sur les canaux Telegram de Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters. ShinyHunters fait partie de ce collectif apparu en 2025, dont les membres ont revendiqué en septembre de la même année la cyberattaque contre Jaguar Land Rover. Le constructeur a dû interrompre sa production pendant des semaines, pour un coût de plus de 220 millions de dollars.
Deux mois plus tard, Brian Krebs a établi l'identité du pirate après avoir analysé des journaux de logiciels voleurs d’informations et échangé avec lui sur Signal. D’après le journaliste, Saif al-Din Khader avait 15 ans et vivait à Amman, en Jordanie. Il a juré avoir pris ses distances avec le groupe. « Je coopère déjà avec les forces de l’ordre. En fait, je leur parle depuis au moins juin », a-t-il écrit, sans que Brian Krebs puisse vérifier ces affirmations.
ShinyHunters a malgré tout poursuivi ses attaques en 2026. En avril, le groupe a volé des millions de documents commerciaux à Rockstar Games, puis il s’en est pris à la plateforme éducative Canvas, au point de perturber en mai les cours de milliers d’écoles américaines. Les polices du monde entier ont du mal depuis des années à arrêter les membres de ces groupes. Avec des pirates aussi jeunes, les poursuites sont complexes, ont expliqué des sources à Reuters, d’autant que les victimes d’extorsion refusent souvent d’aider les enquêteurs.

articles.title: Creíamos que los Wari conquistaron a los Nazca por la fuerza, pero cuatro momias no "dicen" lo mismo
articles.text:
A veces, basta un hallazgo para reescribir lo que creíamos saber de una civilización. Durante siglos, los profesionales de la historia han trazado los límites de las culturas pasadas y sus interacciones a partir de lo que dejaron: construcciones, objetos, cuerpos. Y entonces aparecen cuatro momias intactas en Huaca del Loro, un gran yacimiento de la costa sur de Perú y obligan a replantearse cosas. Durante décadas hemos creído que los wari habían sometido a los nazca por la fuerza, pero el lugar del enterramiento de estos cuerpos apuntan a algo más complejo: a alianzas, diplomacia y colaboraciones.
El hallazgo. En 2022 aparecieron las cuatro momias en ese yacimiento de la civilización nazca, que vivió en la región entre los años 1 y 750 d. C. Estaban envueltas en tejidos, sentadas con las rodillas al pecho y con las manos junto a la cara.
Lo llamativo de todo esto era dónde estaban: en lugar de haberlos encontrado en el cementerio, como el resto, estaban junto a un templo ceremonial wari. Es decir, que no los enterraron como a prisioneros o enemigos, sino colocados en una infraestructura sagrada del pueblo invasor.
Por qué importa. Este descubrimiento cuestiona la idea de que los wari conquistaron a los nazca mediante la violencia y la fuerza militar. Si cuatro personas de la cultura nazca fueron enterradas con cuidado junto a un edificio imperial, entonces quizá la expansión wari incluyó también cooperación e intereses compartidos. La antropóloga biológica Corina Kellner de la Universidad de Arizona del Norte e investigadora lo resume así para Phys: la colonización no siempre es un proceso brutal, porque hay otras formas de influir en una región.
UN VISTAZO A...
Breves apuntes sobre civilizaciones prehispánicas en los Andes. Los nazca, famosos por sus geoglifos y sus acueductos subterráneos, ocuparon la costa sur de Perú aproximadamente entre el año 1 y el 750 d. C. Después llegó el Horizonte Medio (hacia el 600-1000 d. C.), un periodo de transición que marcó el final de su civilización y el inicio de la influencia estatal del Imperio wari y de Tiwanaku, en Bolivia. Los wari se asentaron en Ayacucho, en la sierra, donde cultivar algodón era difícil, mientras que los nazca vivían en tierras más bajas, aptas para el algodón y la coca.
Históricamente se pensaba que los wari sometieron a las comunidades costeras de los nazca por la fuerza: hay estudios que apuntan a que Nazca estuvo gobernada por los wari, pero no está claro cuál fue su verdadero papel en la región.
No eran prisioneros ni enemigos. Que esas personas estuvieran junto a un templo wari y no en el cementerio apunta a un trato diferente, probablemente porque gozaban de prestigio en la sociedad, si bien los análisis de ADN, tomografías e isótopos pendientes arrojarán más información. Eso sí, no todo apunta a la armonía: a poca distancia está Zorropata, un sitio claramente defensivo, con murallas y piedras para hondas, donde se excavó una ofrenda de cabezas trofeo de estilo nazca. Cooperación y conflicto no son excluyentes, y es posible que convivieran.
Según el resumen del proyecto, Huaca del Loro es un asentamiento wari con un cementerio de prácticas híbridas nazca y wari, y un templo en forma de D, uno de los primeros identificados en la costa peruana, según una presentación del proyecto recogida por Gizmodo. ¿Qué pudo unir a ambas sociedades? Un estudio previo de Kellner y Schoeninger plantea que a los wari pudo atraerles la tecnología cerámica nazca. En el estudio actual, Kellner añade los textiles, ya que los wari necesitaban algodón.
Portada | Jerod Roberts y Northern Arizona University

articles.title: YouTube en Argentina: la lista de los 10 videos más vistos este sábado
articles.text:
Con 17 años de vida, YouTube se ha convertido en la plataforma de videos más famosa del mundo y es que en estos días no sólo sirve a los usuarios para ver clips musicales o graciosos, sino que también es empleada por muchos para ver tutoriales y aprender, para conciliar el sueño con los famosos ASMR, visitar otros países a través de diversos videobloggers y mucho más.
Aunque YouTube ha visto nacer plataformas que le han querido hacer la competencia —como Dailymotion, Vimeo y las propias redes sociales Instagram, Facebook y TikTok—, el sitio web de origen estadounidense continúa en el gusto de los internautas, lo que lo ha llevado a ser el segundo sitio más buscado sólo detrás de Google.
En este panorama, YouTube lanzó en el año 2018 su propia sección de tendencias en donde los usuarios pueden ver los nuevos videos musicales que gozan de gran popularidad en tiempo real en 61 países, ello con la finalidad de que no se pierdan ninguno de los clips más importantes, pues se estima que cada minuto son subidos más de 500 horas de contenido mientras que al día son vistos alrededor de 5 mil millones de videos.
Aquí el listado de los 10 artistas y sus canciones más populares del momento
1. 1AmorArtista/canal: Lali
2. Lali, Tini, Marilina Bertoldi - Like A Virgin (EN VIVO) River - Buenos Aires 2026Artista/canal: Lali
3. Cuarteto Sessions 7 (En Vivo)Artista/canal: Q' Lokura
4. NecioArtista/canal: Romeo Santos
5. A QUIEN LE IMPORTA (VERSION CUARTETO)Artista/canal: Luck Ra
6. WANDA NARAArtista/canal: Martin Vegas y La Joaqui
7. Alma de Rezabaile (Casa Sole) (Official Video)Artista/canal: Soledad
8. COLOCARTELO REMIX - RENZO ED X LA JOAQUI X SALASTKBRON X ELAGGUME (Official Music Video)Artista/canal: Renzo ED y elaggume
9. Emanero, Bandana - Ojo de loca (Official video)Artista/canal: Emanero
10. hIGhLIGhTSArtista/canal: Paulo Londra
El boom de Youtube
YouTube vio la luz en febrero de 2005, cuando tres antiguos empleados de la compañía de Paypal ―Chad Hurley, Steve Chen y Jawed Karim― se unieron y la crearon luego de que experimentaran dificultades para compartir entre sí un par de videos tras asistir a una fiesta.
El dominio fue activado el 14 de febrero de 2005 y casi un mes después, el 23 de abril, fue cargado el primer clip a la plataforma que llevaba por nombre “Me at the Zoo”. Fue cuestión de tiempo para que todo el mundo comenzara a cargar contenido y a compartir los enlaces a través de otras redes sociales como MySpace.
Una de las grandes empresas que vio el potencial de YouTube fue la marca Nike, que subió una publicidad protagonizada por Ronaldinho, lo que hizo que otras grandes compañías voltearan a ver a YouTube y se sintieran atraídas.
Tal fue la gran acogida de los internautas por YouTube que para diciembre de 2005 la plataforma pasó de las 50 millones de visitas al día a 250 millones de visualizaciones luego de que un canal subiera el clip musical Lazy Sunday, transmitido originalmente por Saturday Night Live.
Para el año siguiente, en el 2006, el sitio fue comparado por el gigante del internet, Google, por un valor de 1650 millones de dólares. En ese entonces eran visualizados 100 millones de videos al día y 65 mil clips se añadían a diario. También firmaron acuerdos con disqueras para poder reproducir videos musicales.
El impacto de YouTube
Desde que fue puesto en marcha, YouTube fue un sitio que llegó a hacer una revolución no sólo en internet, sino también en la forma en la que los usuarios miran contenido. Muestra de ello el reconocimiento que la revista Time le otorgó en noviembre del 2006 al ser nombrado el “Invento del Año”.
Convertido en el mejor medio de difusión, el gozar de tanta popularidad también ha metido a sus dueños en aprietos como cuando albergar peleas escolares o en donde hay bullying, clips relacionados al terrorismo, narcotráfico u otros temas considerados delicados por su contenido íntimo o por mostrar delitos como asesinatos y más.
Para Estados Unidos uno de los temas más delicados es el de los tiroteos escolares, por lo que YouTube ha estado más de una vez en el ojo del huracán por alojar contenido filmado por los atacantes, como fue el caso de la masacre de Virginia Tech, cuando Cho Seung-Hui, el atacante, subió previamente a los hechos un discurso.
Más recientemente, tras el surgimiento de la pandemia del coronavirus, también ha surgido inquietud sobre cómo la plataforma permite la monetización de contenido que puede ser engañoso y riesgoso para la población.
Aunque no todo es malo, pues a través de dicha plataforma muchas personas han podido ser reconocidas por su talento, como fue el caso de Susan Boyle, quien participó en el programa Britain’s Got Talent cuyo extracto subido a YouTube logró que la mujer pasara a ser una completa desconocida a una de las personas más viralizadas, famosas y aclamadas del internet.

articles.title: Asus built a massive Wi-Fi 8 router nobody can fully test yet
articles.text:
There isn't a single Wi-Fi 8 device on the market, yet this Asus router is already outperforming everything you currently own — here's what you need to know
Asus's new Wi-Fi 8 beast gives your Wi-Fi 7 device an advantage
Asus has beaten every other manufacturer to market with the ROG Rapture GT-BN98, the world's first commercially available Wi-Fi 8 gaming router.
It's a bold flagship release for a wireless standard that isn't even finalized yet — and with zero Wi-Fi 8 client devices currently on sale, reviewers had to get creative just to test what it can actually do. I dug into three in-depth reviews to see whether it's worth buying now.
What reviews say
Build quality drew consistent praise. It's "extremely well constructed with very good attention to detail," said Blacktubi, while Guru3D leaned into the router's dramatic looks, joking that unboxing it feels like "a small alien spacecraft has crash-landed on the desk."
YouTuber Landpet was blunt about the performance side, calling it flat-out "an absolute beast of a router."
On paper, the GT-BN98's theoretical link rates are identical to its Wi-Fi 7 predecessor, the GT-BE98 — Blacktubi pointed out the headline numbers "are the exact same." But real-world range and throughput told a different story.
Design
The chassis is large by any standard. It measures roughly 35cm by 35cm and weighs over 2kg. It needs "a proper, dedicated spot" rather than a small shelf, and ruling out wall mounting altogether given the size.
The antennas dominate the look, adjustable around the perimeter and giving the router an almost insect-like silhouette when fully extended. The top panel mixes a metallic finish with geometric detailing and translucent panels, plus the expected Aura RGB lighting.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Build quality feels solid throughout — no flex, clean panel fit, antenna arms that hold their position. Front-edge LEDs give a quick status read without opening the app.
Thermally, this Asus router added a thicker aluminum top plate and an upgraded heatsink layer for passive cooling. Stress testing turned up no signs of throttling.
Design & ports
Inside is a 2.6GHz quad-core processor and 2GB of RAM, running a quad-band radio setup — 2.4GHz, dual 5GHz bands, and a single 6GHz band — for a combined theoretical throughput of 25,000Mbps.
A North America-only "Pro" variant swaps the second 5GHz band for an extra 6GHz band on the UNII-8 spectrum, which isn't approved for use in most other regions.
For wired gear, there are two 10GbE ports (one general-purpose, one dedicated gaming port), four 2.5GbE ports, and a single gigabit port, with up to six LAN ports active depending on configuration. USB 3.2 Gen1 and USB 2.0 round things out for network storage or 4G/5G backup internet.
Performance
Real-world speed testing — done entirely with Wi-Fi 7 client devices, since Wi-Fi 8 hardware doesn't exist yet — found wired and wireless backhaul holding up strongly even at 100 feet away
Over a wired 10G connection, speeds matched his 5 Gbps ISP plan exactly in both directions. On Wi-Fi, internet speeds hit 4.1 Gbps down and 2 Gbps up.
Local network testing — where speed isn't capped by the ISP — pushed even higher: 4.6 Gbps down and 4.2 Gbps up over wireless backhaul between two mesh units, with wired backhaul close behind at 4.5 Gbps down and 4.2 Gbps up.
Range held up well too. At 20ft, speeds stayed around 4 Gbps down; at 50ft outdoors, 2.7 Gbps down; and even at 100ft, it still managed 1.92 Gbps down, though upload dropped sharply to 718 Mbps.
A more controlled comparison, pairing two GT-BN98 units against two GT-BE98 units, found "significantly higher" throughput at long range with the newer hardware.
The more surprising finding: those gains aren't limited to future Wi-Fi 8 gear. Testing with an existing Wi-Fi 7 MacBook still measured "more than 10% higher average throughput" on the GT-BN98 versus the older Wi-Fi router — evidence that upgraded radio components benefit today's devices too, even without any Wi-Fi 8 features actually switched on.
Firmware
The ASUSWRT 6.0 was singled out as a real step up, with the interface "noticeably more modern and much more responsive" than Asus's decade-old firmware.
The headline addition is the new Adaptive QoE engine, which "smartly allocates network resources to balance gaming, streaming, and daily tasks," replacing the older Adaptive QoS system.
Security also got an upgrade via the revamped AiProtection suite, which was called "genuinely impressive" for including network-level ad and tracker blocking at no extra cost.
The new Wi-Fi Insight tool also correctly flagged interference from a Zigbee smart home devices on the 2.4GHz band, a decent addition which impressively “works as intended”.
Price
Pricing is still rolling out region by region ahead of the router's wider October 2026 launch.
The flagship GT-BN98 Pro is currently the only model on sale, listed on ASUS's Canadian eStore at CA$1,299.99.
A US launch price of around $899 has been floated by early previews but isn't yet official.
The standard GT-BN98 (non-Pro) has also been priced at €960 in Europe, though North American pricing for that specific model hasn't been confirmed yet.
Given the router is shipping ahead of Wi-Fi 8's official IEEE finalization — not expected until 2028 — buyers are paying an early-adopter premium on top of already-flagship router pricing.
Who should buy it
This is a router for enthusiasts buying ahead of the curve, not something you need for Wi-Fi 8 today — compatible client devices aren't expected until 2027 at the earliest.
Still, the benefits aren't purely theoretical: better range, backhaul speed, and firmware improvements apply right now, even to existing Wi-Fi 7 devices.
Verdict
The good
- Meaningfully better range and throughput, even on older Wi-Fi 7 devices
- Premium build quality with no thermal throttling under load
- Adaptive QoE and free-included ad/tracker blocking are genuine upgrades
The bad
- No Wi-Fi 8 client devices exist yet to fully prove the standard
- Large footprint requires dedicated desk space
- High price tag
The verdict
Worth it if you want the best router hardware available today and don't mind future-proofing ahead of the Wi-Fi 8 ecosystem. Hold off if you're not running multi-gig internet or don't need flagship-level range right now.

articles.title: Modder brings support for decade-old Nvidia Pascal GPUs to 24-year-old Windows XP 32-bit — modded drivers unlock better DisplayPort and HDMI support for modern monitors
articles.text:
Modder brings support for decade-old Nvidia Pascal GPUs to 24-year-old Windows XP 32-bit — modded drivers unlock better DisplayPort and HDMI support for modern monitors
Bringing high-performance cards to retro gaming systems.
One of the many appeals of retrocomputing and emulation is being able to play your old games on much better systems than you or your parents could afford at the time. Along those lines, techie SupraGSX has brought support for Nvidia's Pascal-era cards (mainly 10-series and Quadro P2000-P6000 cards) to Windows XP 32-bit, with a bevy of modern accouterments for DisplayPort and HDMI handling, too.
The new ForceWare 382.69 (custom numbering) is a spin-off of the existing 368.81 driver, seemingly Nvidia's last Windows XP release that supported 9-series GPUs. The software also pulls card firmware from Quadro 376.84 drivers, and support for Video Protected Region from Windows 7 GeForce 378.78. Although some websites mention that this project was vibe-coded, the repository doesn't mention it, and a cursory look at the build instructions didn't reveal any obvious traces of clanker activity.
Here's the full list of supported cards, taken from the code repository. The one notable omission is GT 1030, based on the GP108 chip. The rest of the lineup is fairly complete, and there's even an experimental build that supports the 1050 Ti. Since the author is releasing new versions as we speak, it's worth checking the project's README for updated information.
- GeForce GTX 970, 980, 980 Ti; GTX TITAN X (Maxwell).
- GeForce GTX 1060 (3/5/6 GB), 1070, 1070 Ti, 1080, 1080 Ti; TITAN X (Pascal), TITAN Xp.
- GeForce GTX 1050 Ti (experimental support)
- Quadro M4000, M5000, M6000, M6000 24GB; P2000, P2200, P4000, P5000, P6000.
- Additional desktop OEM variants of GTX 950 and GTX 960.
Because contemporary displays with high refresh rates and resolutions can be tricky, SupraGSX added DisplayPort HBR2 and HBR3 support (High Bit Rate), HDMI 2.0 identification and mode-retry fail-safes, HDMI/DVI handling, and improved scaling and aspect ratio settings in the Nvidia Control Panel.
Some folks have tested the new driver, and it appears to work mostly fine, with reports of it working well with ultrawide screens at high refresh rates. SupraGSX is active in the Vogons forums, where it seems to take bug reports and feature requests.
If you're interested in revitalizing your retro system with Forceware, you can go to the project's releases section and download the installer package. Enterprising modders can review the extensive build instructions and perhaps roll their own mods.
Since many retro-tinkerers may be asking for Windows XP 64-bit support, a fork of the Forceware driver existed, but it's since been deleted. However, its binaries live on at Mega. Since these are all unofficial drivers, always exercise caution and don't install them on systems where you're concerned about data safety.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: PanIIT, Andhra Pradesh plan Rs 500 Cr deeptech fund, target 25 AP startups by 2030
articles.text:
PanIIT, Andhra Pradesh plan Rs 500 Cr deeptech fund, target 25 AP startups by 2030
The proposed fund is part of a broader PanIIT-Andhra Pradesh push to build a deeptech ecosystem in the state. Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu told venture capital investors that the state would match their contribution to deeptech investments.
PanIIT Alumni India and the Andhra Pradesh government plan to create a ₹500-crore venture fund focused on deeptech companies, as part of a broader effort to channel capital, research and manufacturing activity into the state.
The proposed PanIIT Amaravati Venture Fund will seek capital from IIT alumni, industry and institutional investors and is targeting its first close by July 1, 2027, according to plans presented at the PanIIT Andhra Pradesh Summit in Vijayawada on Saturday.
The fund aims to back at least 25 Andhra Pradesh-based deeptech ventures by 2030.
The precise structure of the fund, including the respective financial commitments of PanIIT, the Andhra Pradesh government and private investors, was not immediately clear.
Principal R&D or manufacturing in AP
At least 50% of the companies the fund invests in will be expected to locate their principal R&D or manufacturing operations in Andhra Pradesh, according to material presented at the conference.
The localisation requirement is designed to ensure that the proposed fund does more than invest in companies headquartered elsewhere, by tying a significant part of its portfolio to research or manufacturing activity within the state.
Speaking to a panel of venture capital investors at the summit, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu made a direct pitch for investors to bring both capital and expertise.
“You bring money, you bring mentors. I will match your contribution,” Naidu said.
The precise mechanism through which the state would match private contributions, and whether the commitment would flow directly into the PanIIT Amaravati Venture Fund, was not immediately clear.
The proposed fund seeks to address two constraints that frequently confront deeptech startups: access to patient capital and access to experienced operators and industry networks.
Deeptech companies typically face longer product-development cycles and greater capital requirements than software-first startups, particularly in areas such as semiconductors, quantum technologies, aerospace, defence, healthcare and advanced manufacturing.
Amaravati Declaration
The venture fund sits within a broader framework laid out under the Andhra PanIIT Declaration, which seeks to create a long-term institutional relationship between the IIT ecosystem, industry and the Andhra Pradesh government.
Among the proposed initiatives is a permanent PanIIT Amaravati Council, which is expected to act as a coordinating platform for deeptech, research and innovation initiatives in the state.
The framework also includes a technology-transfer pipeline to identify research from IITs that can be commercialised in Andhra Pradesh, a 100-member global IIT mentor network and 10 industry chairs across universities and institutions in the state.
The Amaravati Council is intended to connect IIT alumni, startups, universities, industry and policymakers and provide a more permanent structure for initiatives emerging from the summit.
The broader framework also seeks to deepen collaboration between universities and industry, support startup creation and make it easier for research developed within the IIT ecosystem to move towards commercial deployment.
It also sets a target of incubating at least 50 startups in Andhra Pradesh by 2030.
IIT mentor network
PanIIT is looking to build a mentor network alongside the fund. A proposed 100-member Global IIT Mentor Networkis expected to connect founders with IIT alumni who can provide guidance across product development, go-to-market strategy, scaling and execution.
An initial cohort of 25 deeptech startups is expected to be matched with mentors, according to plans presented at the summit.
The mentor network is intended to complement the proposed venture fund by bringing operating experience and industry connections alongside capital.
Taken together, the fund, mentor network and Amaravati Declaration mark an attempt to link venture capital with IIT research and alumni expertise, while using Andhra Pradesh as a base for startup creation, R&D and manufacturing.

articles.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
President Donald Trump hosted many of the biggest names in artificial intelligence this week — in part to announce that the U.S. government isn’t calling it artificial intelligence anymore. Now it’s super intelligence.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the motivation behind the meeting and what effect it might have on the AI industry. We were all pretty skeptical that the “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” that the executives signed will amount to much, especially since — as Sean noted — it’s “deeply non-binding,” at least from a legal prospective. (Instead, Trump said he considers it “morally binding.”)
Kirsten suggested that the meeting’s real significance may have been as “a rebranding effort around AI.” (An effort that continued this weekend with Trump’s announcement of a new Super Intelligence Force.) For her, the big message was, “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs — but super intelligence is not.”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Anthony Ha: Officially, by order of the president of the United States, it’s not artificial intelligence anymore, it’s super intelligence. We were talking about this last week, because this is something [Trump has] been hinting at — he doesn’t do hints, he’s been saying [it] for a while. But now it’s signed into executive order. If you’re an official U.S. representative, you are supposed to say super intelligence, not artificial intelligence.
And this was also part of this broader announcement around AI safety, which I think is both interesting for this pact that was announced, but also the fact that it happened at all. It seemed to have come together fairly quickly, because just two weeks ago, a week ago, President Trump was saying, “We don’t need any of this, we need to lead in AI, we can’t constrain it in any way, we don’t need any regulation, anyone who’s saying that there’s any danger from AI is essentially a Chinese or Democratic plant.” And yet all these AI CEOs got together with him earlier this week and signed this pact.
Kirsten Korosec: Leading up to that, we should say, not only was there pushback on regulation, and we can talk about whether this executive order even does any of that — I would say no, there’s a little bit of theater there — but the important and interesting thing is that just days ago, Anthropic was really in the doghouse, if you will, in terms of what was happening behind the scenes with President Trump.
That all changed when [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei was invited to a 10 p.m. dinner. He had this sit-down, and then just days later, we had this luncheon, and at this luncheon, we have pretty much every tech power broker from every major tech company that exists. So Mark Zuckerberg was there, Jeff Bezos was there, Elon Musk was there, Dario of course was there, they were all there.
I’m wondering if any of you watched the press conference that happened afterwards, which there’s been many, many memes about, because of the interesting, funny behavior when you bring a bunch of tech CEOs together.
But I guess my bigger question for both of you is: What does this all mean? And does it mean anything?
Sean O’Kane: How much time do you have? First off, sure, they had dinner, Trump and Dario. If you read the Time magazine interview that Trump just did, your guess is as good as mine as to how informed he was that that dinner was even going to be happening, which is a strange reality to live in, but it’s just the one we inhabit.
I will also say one other thing that makes me skeptical — surprise, surprise — of how repaired the relationship is between the administration and Anthropic, is that for as much as there are clearly people trying to put those two groups together, the Defense Department is still very adamant that Anthropic is terrible and woke and and a national security risk. Emil Michael goes off on Anthropic every other day on X, it seems. I think there’s still some distance there despite Dario showing up to this thing.
As far as the agreement and all of that, let’s be real, they misspelled the United States on the agreement that they all signed. It is also just deeply non-binding. I mean, it is completely voluntary. I think my favorite aspect about it was that Trump described it as quote “morally binding,” which is just a level of abstraction and terminology that I’ve never heard of before.
Anthony: In terms of Anthropic and their relationship with the Trump administration, there’s been a sort of a lot of reporting, especially during that big blow up with the Defense Department, that different parts of the White House had different relationships with Anthropic. The Treasury Secretary seemed to be a big fan, whereas the Defense Department — definitely not big fans, or at least unhappy with some of the conditions that Anthropic were trying to put on the use of their technology.
In that sense, it feels like nothing has necessarily changed. There are people in the White House who want to use Anthropic’s technology, want them involved in these decisions, and others who really, really, really, really don’t.
In terms of the agreement, it seems not super meaningful. What is meaningful is just the fact that they felt that this was something worth doing. As indicated by the fact that they misspelled United States, it seemed like they rushed to put all of this together. [But] the fact that this kind of gesture was needed seems significant, even if I don’t think the agreement itself is going to lead to any major changes.
Kirsten: I do think that there was one important thing that happened. And to me, this is the point of it, which was a rebranding exercise around AI. “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs, but super intelligence is not.” This isn’t my personal belief. To me, that was the message.

articles.title: YouTube en Colombia: la lista de los 10 videos más reproducidos que son tendencia hoy
articles.text:
Desde su aparición en el 2005, YouTube se ha convertido en uno de los sitios web más importantes en la vida moderna, llegando a ser un fenómeno global que revolucionó la forma en la que se consume el contenido audiovisual.
Pese a que otras redes sociales como TikTok, Facebook o Instagram están apostando cada vez más por los videos, lo cierto es que YouTube sigue siendo el rey y para prueba de ello las cifras: es el segundo sitio electrónico más visitado en el mundo sólo detrás de Google; además tiene presencia en 104 países y está disponible en 80 idiomas.
Asimismo, a la plataforma estadounidense se suben alrededor de 500 horas de contenido por minuto y se cree que al día son vistos cinco mil millones de videos, dejando ganancias estimadas de 15 mil millones de dólares al trimestre.
Ante la facilidad que tienen los usuarios para perderse en un mundo de clips, Youtube ha creado diversas listas para consultar a los artistas más escuchados, más vistos y cuáles son las tendencias del día en tiempo real.
Estos son los videos que están en tendencia este sábado 3 de octubre
1. NecioArtista/canal: Romeo Santos
2. PARADIXE (Visualizer)Artista/canal: El Americano 4KT, Pirlo y Feid
3. Yeison Jiménez & Nico Hernández l Bandido Retirado (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Nico Hernández
4. COMPA COLETO (uy_como)Artista/canal: ARIA VEGA
5. versAAce | CARABIN3 ft ANUEL AA (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: CARABIN3 Oficial
6. Chucky73 x TOPBOY x El Americano 4KT - MAS BONITO (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Chucky73
7. Peli De Terror - Koddy G (VIDEO OFICIAL)Artista/canal: Køddy G
8. Ricardo Arjona y Grupo Firme - Amor Factura (Video Oficial) ArjonaOficial GrupoFirmeOficialArtista/canal: Ricardo Arjona
9. YO QUIERO RMX Hades66, Arcángel, Myke Towers, Luar La L- (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Hades 66
10. FANTA ROSARIO, Kris R. - DE MEDALLO PA MOROVIS (Visualizer)Artista/canal: FANTA ROSARIO
Los favoritos de los colombianos en el 2023
La plataforma de YouTube se ha mantenido entre las más populares a pesar de la diversificación de opciones para consumir vídeos y música. Los usuarios la usan para ver videos musicales, tutoriales y hasta noticias. Respecto a los artistas que más vieron este 2023, en el primer lugar estuvo Karol G y Shakira con TQG; en segundo lugar Joaquin Guiller, Maycol Rosero, Beren con No Sufriré Por Nadie; en seguida, Yng Lvcas y Peso Pluma con el videoclip de La Bebe.
La plataforma también ha sido testigo de la creciente popularidad de creadores de contenido latinoamericanos a lo largo de 2023. Entre ellos, se destaca el influencer uruguayo Fede Vigevani, quien se ha consolidado como uno de los youtubers más vistos en Colombia.
El contenido de Vigevani se caracteriza por su versatilidad, abarcando desde vlogs, retos, hasta bromas en cámara oculta. Otro creador que ha acaparado la atención en la región es el estadounidense MrBeast, conocido por sus desafíos y sorteos. A pesar de ser un creador de contenido que no es de habla hispana, MrBeast ha logrado trascender las barreras del idioma y se ha posicionado entre los más vistos en Colombia.
A estos creadores se suman Alfredo Larin, Ian Lucas, Ami Rodríguez y como “revelación del año”: Alextis, The Donato, Albertisment, Amara Que Linda y DeGoBooM. Estos creadores han demostrado que es posible alcanzar una gran audiencia fuera de sus países de origen, a la par de poner en alto el idioma español en la plataforma, donde comunidades de habla hispana continúan creciendo y consumiendo contenido.
Mientras que en los videos más populares, demostraron que les interesa más el entretenimiento y lo noticioso. Los más reproducidos fueron: Rihanna’s FULL Apple Music Super Bowl LVII Halftime Show; ES LEY: Ni se te ocurra hacer la TÉCNICO-MECÁNICA sin saber esto $$$; $1 vs $500,000 Plane Ticket! - $1 vs $500,000 Plane Ticket!; The Juanpis Live Show - Entrevista a F***s News y Millonarios 1 (3) vs Nacional 1 (2) - El ‘Embajador’ hace historia al ganar la estrella 16.

articles.title: Why did Virat Kohli give up a Rs 300 Cr Puma deal to back Abhishek Ganguly’s Agilitas?
articles.text:
Why did Virat Kohli give up a Rs 300 Cr Puma deal to back Abhishek Ganguly’s Agilitas?
In this episode of the Prime Venture Partners Podcast, Abhishek Ganguly shares how he built Puma India, how Virat Kohli’s one8 came about, and what Agilitas is trying to build in India’s sportswear market?
For 17 years, Abhishek Ganguly helped build one of the biggest sportswear success stories in India.
When he joined Puma in 2005, he was the second employee in the country. The company did not even have an Indian entity, and its early team worked out of a Coffee World in Koramangala, Bengaluru, attracted partly by the free internet. Puma would eventually become one of the first single brands in fashion and sportswear to cross Rs 1,500 crore and then Rs 2,000 crore in revenue in India. Ganguly says it went on to become bigger than Nike and Adidas put together in the country.
Perhaps even more striking was the capital behind that growth. According to Ganguly, by 2023, Puma India had put in only around $20 million in equity capital to build a business generating roughly $400 million in revenue.
But when Ganguly decided to start Agilitas Sports, he realised that nearly two decades of experience could be as much a liability as an advantage.
“What got Puma to where it got will not get Agilitas even an inch ahead,” he told Amit Somani, Managing Partner at Prime Venture Partners, on the Prime Venture Partners Podcast.
Why India needs a different sportswear company
The idea behind Agilitas came partly from something Ganguly had noticed during his years working for a global sportswear company.
At Puma’s headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Germany, meeting rooms carried the names of cities including Barcelona, New York, Los Angeles, Tokyo, Melbourne and Seoul.
“No New Delhi, no Bangalore,” he recalls.
Rather than viewing it as a complaint, Ganguly saw an opportunity. Despite the growth of the Indian market, India did not yet have what he calls a “pride of place” in global sportswear.
Countries such as the US and Germany had created global sports brands of their own. China had built its own brands too. Ganguly began asking a simple question: why not India?
That question would eventually become central to Agilitas.
“We always didn't want to be a brand for India. We wanted to be a brand from India,” he says.
The distinction matters. Ganguly does not want Agilitas to compete by positioning Indian products as cheaper alternatives to international brands. His ambition is to build products that can compete with the best globally on their own terms.
“This will compete with the best in the world,” he says of the company's products.
‘Consumers don’t need more brands’
Building that company, however, requires understanding how dramatically the Indian consumer has changed.
Two decades ago, Ganguly says, consumers were reluctant to spend Rs 5,000 to Rs 6,000 on a pair of shoes.
Today, sneaker culture has reached a point where he knows people in India who own as many as 400 pairs.
Retail has transformed alongside the consumer. India moved from limited offline retail to mono-brand stores, ecommerce and now quick commerce. Consumers who once struggled to access international brands can today choose from an enormous range of products.
That creates a very different problem for a company like Agilitas.
“Consumers don't need more products, they don't need more brands, they don't need more retail,” Ganguly says.
Availability alone is no longer differentiation. Neither is simply making another good shoe. Brands increasingly need to give consumers a reason to pay attention to them.
Ganguly borrows a framework from social media to explain how he thinks about this. Instagram, he says, taught brands that content first needs to be “scroll stopping” and then good enough to be shared.
“So there is a scroll stopping behavior and then you have to build which is shareable,” he says. “Scroll stopping means you got the attention, then you were good enough that people shared.”
For Agilitas, the challenge is therefore not simply making products. It is earning consideration in a market where consumers already have plenty of choices.
Why experience can become a founder’s biggest risk
Perhaps Ganguly's most counterintuitive belief about building Agilitas is that his previous success does not necessarily give the company an advantage.
It could do precisely the opposite.
“The biggest risk Agilitas has is because I have done this before,” he says.
His reasoning is that successful operators can become prisoners of their own pattern recognition. What worked previously starts looking like a template for what should work again. Confidence can turn into certainty, and certainty can reduce the willingness to learn.
“If you think you know it, you build ego and you're low on learning,” he says.
Ganguly has a phrase he says he reminds himself of every day: “Disruptors don't disrupt again.”
The lesson has become particularly relevant because of the speed at which Indian consumption is changing. Ganguly says his first two-and-a-half to three years building Agilitas have already taught him things that run counter to lessons from his previous 20 years in the industry.
Consumers are evolving too quickly, he argues, for history alone to provide the answers.
From Virat Kohli the ambassador to Virat Kohli the builder
One of the most visible manifestations of the Agilitas strategy is its relationship with Virat Kohli.
The relationship goes back to 2016, when Kohli was Indian cricket captain and coming off an extraordinary IPL season. Ganguly, then at Puma, proposed something different from the conventional celebrity endorsement model.
Rather than simply paying Kohli a fixed brand ambassador fee, he suggested building a brand that belonged to Kohli, which could collaborate with Puma through a royalty arrangement. That relationship eventually developed into One8.
Years later, when Ganguly was preparing to leave Puma, Kohli was among the first people he told.
Ganguly explained his ambition to create a sportswear company from India. The conversation returned to the same question behind Agilitas: “Why not us?”
“Why can't an Indian brand get to the podium of the Olympics?” Ganguly recalls them asking. Why could a brand from India not eventually become the preferred choice of athletes elsewhere in the world?
Kohli subsequently became one of Agilitas' early believers. Ganguly says the cricketer walked away from a large financial outlay from Puma, invested in Agilitas and merged his brand with the company.
His role, Ganguly insists, goes considerably beyond lending his name and face to the brand.
When the company was developing its first performance cricket shoe ahead of the IPL, Kohli personally tested the product and rejected 17 prototypes.
“He tested it like, like with schoolboy energy,” Ganguly says, describing Kohli as being involved in the smallest details of the product.
It is an example of what Agilitas wants the relationship to represent. Kohli is not merely the celebrity used to generate attention for a finished product. He is part of the process of building it.
Building something that eventually outgrows its founders
The long-term ambition is bigger than any individual associated with the company.
Ganguly recalls asking Kohli what success for One8 would look like 20 years from now. Kohli's answer surprised him.
Success, he said, would be when “nobody cares two hoots about who built this, who started this.”
For Ganguly, that reflected a “deep builder mindset”.
It also fits his own decision to start again.
Ganguly grew up, he says, in an India where success was often associated with certainty and stability. People were encouraged to find a path and eventually “settle down”. Over time, he discovered that the moments he enjoyed most came from moving away from what had already been built and attempting something that had not been done before.
“I want to stay unfinished till I can,” he says.
For someone who has already spent two decades building in Indian sportswear, Agilitas is therefore less about recreating the last journey than attempting an entirely different one.
And Ganguly's advice to entrepreneurs reflects that distinction.
“Always learn from others. The gateway of the world is through others, but never try to copy others,” he says.
(Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

articles.title: En 2013 un ingeniero indio construyó un glaciar artificial en uno de los desiertos más áridos de la Tierra. 13 años después, la agricultura vive de su invento
articles.text:
Es enero, de madrugada y, en mitad un desierto a más de 3.000 metros de altura, un surtidor escupe agua hacia el cielo. Las gotas no llegan a caer. No como agua. Se congelan en el aire y, capa a capa, noche a noche, van levantando una enorme estructura de hielo de 30 ó 50 metros de altura.
Parece magia, pero las estupas de hielo de Ladakh son algo más: el ser humano luchando no solo contra la sed, sino (sobre todo) contra el calendario.
Pero empecemos por el principio. El Ladakh es un desierto frío al norte de la India. Caen menos de 50 mm de lluvia al año y el 80% de los agricultores vive del agua de los glaciares. Y, dentro de lo que cabe, no les ha ido mal.
El problema es que el deshielo va su ritmo: los glaciares solo empiezan a soltar agua en junio o julio y, sin embargo, lo idóneo sería tener agua en abril o mayo (cuando llega el momento de sembrar). Por contra, los arroyos bajan llenos en invierno, cuando nadie puede aprovecharlos.
Hasta que llegó Chewang Norphel. Eran finales de los 80 y el ingeniero Norphel pensó en que quizás se podía desviar esos arroyos hacia laderas de sombra. Construyeron muretes de piedra y consiguieron congelar buena parte de ese agua en finas láminas (alimentando así las plantaciones de la región).
El ejemplo que siempre se suele poner estaba en Phuktsey, tenía unos 300 metros de largo y daba agua a unas 700 personas. Pero no era perfecto. Necesitaba sombra y una altura suficiente como para que no se derritiera pronto. No era algo fácil de generalizar.
En 2013, dieron un paso adelante. Otro ingeniero Sonam Wangchuk propuso dejar de extender el hielo y empezar a apilarlo. El método de Norphel creaba piscinas poco profundas para almacenar el agua congelada; el de Wangchuk creaba conos que, por su propia estructura, exponían menos hielo al sol. Podían retrasar el deshielo de forma significativa.
Para ponerlo en marcha, crearon una canalización que acercaba el agua a las aldeas y allí creaban grandes conos de hielo para cuando fuera necesario usarlo. El prototipo, de octubre de 2013, medía unos seis metros, guardaba unos 150.000 litros y aguantó congelado hasta el 18 de mayo. Fue tan sorprendente que, en 2017, ya lo contamos aquí.
Pero... ¿qué ha pasado desde entonces? Esta década larga, como reconoce el director del proyecto, Nishant Tiku, han conseguido almacenar algo más de 67 millones de litros de capacidad en 24 aldeas. Sin lugar a dudas, es mucho para un solo asentamiento; pero, en una región de unos 300.000 habitantes, se queda un poco corta.
¿Tiene futuro? Pues no está claro. Hasta donde sabemos, Wangchuk pasó 170 días detenido entre 2025 y 2026, acusado de incitar unas protestas en Leh en las que la policía mató a cuatro personas y, aunque él lo niega, la administración de Ladakh retiró su apoyo a otra de sus iniciativas. Nadie sabe en qué ha quedado todo esto.
Más allá de todo esto, es bonito ver cómo la humanidad no deja nunca de dar vueltas a las mismas ideas. Sea en los desiertos de la India o en las acequias de Sierra Nevada, el mundo sigue luchando con uñas y dientes para que haya agua dónde y cuándo la necesitamos.

articles.title: Nikon réexamine une vidéo scientifique gagnante après des soupçons d’utilisation de l’IA
articles.text:
Nikon a récompensé à la mi-septembre une vidéo de cils respiratoires filmée au microscope. Très vite, des chercheurs ont relevé à l’écran des structures introuvables en biologie. L’un d’eux a même détecté dans la vidéo le filigrane invisible de Google pour les contenus générés par IA. Le constructeur japonais a rouvert le dossier.
Nikon Instruments récompense depuis seize ans, avec son concours Small World in Motion, les plus belles vidéos tournées au microscope optique. Cette année, le jury a donné la première place à Ning Xu, ingénieur en optique aujourd’hui en poste à l’Université nationale de Singapour. Ce chercheur a filmé, par microscopie à super-résolution diffractive, les cils respiratoires d’un enfant atteint de dyskinésie ciliaire primitive. Chez les personnes touchées par cette maladie génétique rare, ces minuscules poils battent de façon anormale et évacuent mal le mucus des bronches, d’où des infections à répétition.
Or Nikon interdit noir sur blanc les vidéos générées par IA dans son règlement, et Ning Xu a admis avoir employé un modèle d’IA après la prise de vue. Les chercheurs qui ont lancé l’alerte interrogent surtout la frontière entre la retouche d’une image scientifique et sa fabrication.
Des structures introuvables en biologie
Quelques jours après la proclamation des résultats, plusieurs spécialistes de la microscopie ont passé la vidéo au crible sur les réseaux sociaux. Edward Phelps, professeur associé en bio-ingénierie à l’université de Floride, a d’abord pointé les formes violettes visibles sous les cils. « Elles ressemblent à des mitochondries, mais une telle structure sous-épithéliale n’existe pas en biologie », a-t-il souligné. À l’écran, ces formes apparaissent et disparaissent d’une image à l'autre, tandis que des cils verts « surgissent de nulle part » et ne correspondent pas à leur taille connue. Nikon n’avait jamais expliqué, dans sa présentation de la vidéo, la nature de ces structures colorées, si bien que le chercheur a réclamé des comptes. « La communauté des microscopistes mérite une explication de la part de Nikon », a-t-il insisté.
Le 22 septembre, Nikon a ajouté sur le blog du concours que Ning Xu avait employé un modèle d’IA « non supervisé » pour l’aider au post-traitement. Ian Donovan, doctorant en médecine et en sciences au centre médical UT Southwestern, au Texas, a de son côté soumis la vidéo à Gemini, avec à la clé la détection d’un filigrane SynthID. Google insère ce marquage invisible dans les images et vidéos créées ou modifiées par ses modèles d’IA, et n’importe quel utilisateur peut vérifier sa présence depuis l’application Gemini.
En cas de résultat positif, tout ou partie du contenu a été créé ou modifié par l’un de ses modèles, précise l’entreprise. Avec ce seul test, impossible de savoir si les cils sont l’œuvre d'un générateur ou s’ils ont seulement été colorés par un outil de Google.
Ning Xu défend une simple mise en couleur
Ning Xu n’a pas répondu à Nature, mais il a publié sa version des faits sur LinkedIn. « L’IA n'a pas servi à générer le film expérimental, les cils ou leur mouvement », a écrit le lauréat. Le modèle a été appliqué après coup aux données reconstruites en niveaux de gris, pour différencier et colorer des structures à la morphologie voisine. Son objectif était d’améliorer la présentation visuelle, sans rien affirmer sur l’anatomie des éléments colorés. Pour lui, mesure et visualisation ont chacune leur rôle. « Les deux peuvent avoir leur place, du moment qu’on sait clairement lequel est lequel », a-t-il ajouté.
Melanie White, biologiste du développement à l’université du Queensland, en Australie, a rappelé que « les images scientifiques ne sont pas de simples illustrations ». « Nous devons pouvoir être sûrs que ce que nous voyons repose sur la mesure sous-jacente », a-t-elle insisté. D’après elle, certaines structures de la vidéo sont peut-être le produit de l’IA, sans existence réelle dans les données de microscopie. Pour Markus Sauer, spécialiste de la microscopie à super-résolution à l'université de Wurtzbourg, en Allemagne, l’IA en visualisation scientifique n’est un problème qu’en cas de résultats expérimentaux déformés ou exagérés. Début septembre, le CNRS pointait d’ailleurs l’usage dissimulé de l'IA générative, et non l'IA elle-même, dans son alerte sur le risque d’effondrement des publications scientifiques mondiales.
Nikon « réexamine attentivement » les éléments fournis lors de la vérification initiale, ainsi que des documents complémentaires transmis par le lauréat. Ning Xu « coopère respectueusement », indique le constructeur, et a remis une documentation technique détaillée sur son microscope et ses méthodes de traitement. Le 1er octobre, ses commentaires LinkedIn étaient toutefois introuvables, et son profil avait été supprimé.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis.
These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land.
Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.
Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.
The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions.
There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders?
It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen.
Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in?
Deals!
Harbinger, the EV startup, landed a $300 million deal to supply FedEx with 2,000 of its electric trucks.
HyperGuest, an Israeli travel tech startup, raised $25 million from AMI, the investment arm of Apax Partners.
REGENT Craft, the developer and manufacturer of the all-electric Seaglider, extended its collaboration with the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab, pushing the total value of the contract to $19.25 million.
Quartermaster, an Arlington, Virginia-based maritime intelligence startup, raised $140 million in a Series B round. About $100 million came from Insight Partners, defense-focused firm Overmatch Ventures, and First Round Capital. The remaining $40 million came in the form of a debt facility from investment bank Stifel.
Voltaback, a French fleet management software startup, raised €2.8 million from European investment fund Serena.
Notable reads and other tidbits
When Aurora announced it would have 30,000 autonomous trucks on the road by the end of 2030, I admit that I raised at least one of my eyebrows. I interviewed CFO David Maday to find out exactly how the company plans to accomplish this and why he’s confident it will succeed.
BMW unveiled its new 2027 3 Series and it’s offering essentially the same car for gas and electric. Guess which one is cheaper?
DoorDash shared more about its new drone delivery business DoorDash Air, including the autonomous aircraft and its ground-based systems approach.
Kodiak has landed Ikea as a customer and will begin driverless deliveries on public highways later this year. The trucks will haul Ikea products without anyone in the cab on a 219-mile stretch of Interstate 45 between Houston and Dallas, according to the company.
Lyft agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle a lawsuit accusing the ride-hailing company of violating California law by misclassifying drivers as independent contractors, instead of employees. The settlement wraps up violations that occurred before Prop 22 was approved by voters, which allows companies like Uber and Lyft to classify drivers as contractors.
Northeastern University tested 21 late-model vehicles from 17 automakers and 30 companion mobile apps. The upshot: cars are collecting a trove of personal data and sharing it with a lot of tech companies, including Adobe, Contentsquare, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Snap, and Yahoo.
SpaceX’s Starship rocket reached Earth orbit for the first time, though not without some drama along the way.
Rivian reported a record-setting quarter of sales thanks to the new R2 SUV. And it’s still forecasting between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles this year. But it is experiencing a few hiccups with its newest EV. The company issued a recall for its R2 SUV over fasteners on its high-voltage battery pack that might not be properly tightened, which can cause a loss of power while driving.
We’ll finish this roundup with a few notable Tesla news item. The company sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, the second strong quarter in a row for the company after a softer start to the year. The company has delayed its Roadster 2 event again due to bad weather.
And while Tesla’s traditional automotive business may be clicking along, it really wants to be considered an AI and robotics company. One year ago, Elon Musk laid out his fourth Master Plan, which he claims will deliver “amazing abundance” through robotaxis, robots, and AI. As Sean O’Kane noted in his recent piece, “What that means, more than a year later, is still tricky to pin down.”
It did just pin down more money to try. The company secured $30 billion in fresh credit lines that could be used to scale its future products, including the Optimus robot and the Cybercab robotaxi.
One more thing …
The countdown begins! Disrupt 2026, TechCrunch’s annual tech conference in San Francisco, is just days away. I mentioned this last week and I am here to share this again. I’m offering you a 30% discount on tickets to Disrupt with code mobility30.
Why go? Well, I am interviewing Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe onstage October 13. I will also interview Mikell Taylor, director of robotics strategy at GM; Shield AI CTO Nathan Michael; and Waabi founder and CEO Raquel Urtasun on a panel entitled “Building AI Systems When Failure Is Not an Option.” Sean O’Kane will interview Also CEO Chris Yu; Yuri Sagalov, managing director at General Catalyst; and Shan Shan, investment manager at Baillie Gifford in “How to Win When You’re Not Building AI.” Plus, hear from execs and engineers from Cerebras, Nvidia, OpenAI, and Replit to name a few.
