articles.title: The Best 1440p QD-OLED Monitors for Less Than $500
articles.text:
Today we're taking a comprehensive look at budget 1440p QD-OLED gaming monitors. This category offers fantastic value at the moment, with plenty of options available below $500. In fact, over the last couple of months we've seen some models drop as low as $300, which is pretty crazy.
For this round-up, we've tested 11 different monitors, including quite a few models we haven't covered before. The goal is to compare the options that matter most and hopefully make it easier to narrow down your buying decision.
Before getting into each monitor, there's one important detail you need to know. When shopping for a 27-inch 1440p QD-OLED, you'll generally encounter three different panel variants, often within a similar price range and sometimes separated by less than $100. All use the same generation of QD-OLED technology, so the fundamental hardware is largely similar across the range. However, the three variants are:
- 1440p, 280Hz, with full brightness capabilities
- 1440p, 240Hz, with full brightness capabilities
- 1440p, 240Hz, with limited brightness capabilities
There's an obvious trap here. Two of these panels run at 240Hz, but one can reach up to 1,000 nits of peak brightness, while the other is limited to just 400 nits.
That's a problem because when you see a 1440p 240Hz QD-OLED listed at a retailer, it isn't immediately obvious which version you're getting. Things become even more confusing when both options are priced similarly. Some brands are also being a little deceptive here, in our view, using very similar names for the full- and limited-brightness variants. That only adds to the confusion when browsing through the available models.
Making matters worse, the limited-brightness panel arrived well after the full-brightness version. QD-OLED established itself as a monitor technology capable of around 1,000 nits of peak brightness, and for a while that was what buyers could expect from essentially every model. Then, somewhat quietly, this nerfed 400-nit panel began appearing on the market.
Throughout this round-up we'll make it clear which monitor uses which panel, but there are also a few ways you can double-check this yourself. One option is our website, Monitor Deals. We've validated the specifications for every product included on the site and clearly identify which panel each monitor uses. Product pages also include a warning when a model has lower brightness than you might expect, while our similar-monitors feature groups together products that use identical panels.
You can also look closely at the manufacturer's spec sheet. The 280Hz panel is always the full-brightness variant. For 240Hz models, full-brightness versions are typically rated for 250 nits of SDR brightness, 1,000 nits peak HDR brightness, and DisplayHDR 400 certification. The limited-brightness models lack DisplayHDR 400 certification and are rated for just 200 nits SDR and 400 nits HDR. If you see those specifications on a product page, you're probably looking at the limited-brightness panel.
A Quick Look at the Monitors
| Monitor | Refresh Rate | Brightness Tier | SDR / Peak HDR | Recent Pricing | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dell Alienware AW2725D | 280Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $400 | 
| MSI MAG 271QP X28 | 280Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $450 | 
| MSI MAG 273QP X24 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | – | 
| MSI MAG 271QPX E2 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $350 | 
| Gigabyte MO27Q2 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | <$600 | 
| Acer Predator X27U X1 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $450 | 
| Dell Alienware AW2726DM | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $350 | 
| Gigabyte GO27Q24A | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $350 | 
| AOC Q27G40ZDF | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | – | 
| Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMES | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $400 | 
| MSI MAG 272QP X24 | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $400 | 
Let's start with the 280Hz models.
The first is the Dell Alienware AW2725D, which we reviewed in 2025. It has an MSRP of $550, but has recently been discounted to $400, and we'd expect to see sales around that price regularly from here on.
The other 280Hz option in this round-up is the MSI MAG 271QP X28, which has an MSRP of $500 but is more typically found for around $450. Both the Dell and MSI models offer the full brightness capabilities of these 1440p QD-OLED panels, reaching up to 1,000 nits peak.
Next are the 240Hz models using full-brightness panels.
For some reason, MSI has produced multiple versions based on this panel, so we've included both the MAG 273QP X24 and the older MAG 271QPX E2. The E2 can occasionally be found for around $350, while the 273QP X24 has been discontinued in some markets. MSI's 271QP X24 is a minor variant of the 273QP X24 with a slightly different design, although we haven't tested that particular model.
The Gigabyte MO27Q2 is another 240Hz full-brightness option, which we reviewed in 2025. It launched at $600 but was frequently sold below that price, and it's still available in some regions despite largely being replaced by the MO27Q2A, which uses a 280Hz panel.
We've also tested the Acer Predator X27U X1, which is commonly found for around $400 to $450. Acer offers several X27U models: the X1 tested here uses the 240Hz full-brightness panel, the Z1 uses the 280Hz panel, and the W1 uses the lower-brightness 240Hz panel.
All three models look very similar, and Acer's naming scheme doesn't make them especially easy to distinguish. For this round-up, though, we're specifically testing the 240Hz X1.
The Lower-Brightness 240Hz Models
Then we get to the 240Hz models using the limited-brightness panel.
One we've already reviewed is the Dell Alienware AW2726DM, which made a huge splash when it launched with an MSRP of just $350. That aggressive price forced a number of other QD-OLED manufacturers to respond and helped push prices down across the category.
We also have the Gigabyte GO27Q24A, which carries an MSRP of $450 but typically sells for around $350, matching the Alienware. Gigabyte has actually done a decent job with its naming scheme here. A G at the beginning indicates the lower-cost, lower-spec variant, while an M indicates a step up with full-brightness capabilities. Just watch the letter at the end. The GO27Q24A is the QD-OLED model, while the GO27Q24G uses a WOLED panel.
The AOC Q27G40ZDF is another low-cost 240Hz QD-OLED, although AOC appears to offer several variants using this limited-brightness panel depending on the retailer and region.
Also in the same family are the Q27G41ZDF and Q27GAZD. All three are extremely similar, so our findings for the G40ZDF should broadly apply to the other two models. Even the design and connectivity are essentially the same.
The ROG Strix XG27AQDMES is Asus' take on the 240Hz limited-brightness panel. It bizarrely launched with an MSRP of $600, though more recently it has been available for around $400.
Lastly, we have the MSI MAG 272QP X24, which also uses the lower-brightness 240Hz panel.
This is where MSI's line-up becomes particularly confusing and, in our opinion, somewhat deceptive. The 272QP X24 and very similar 274QP X24 both use the limited-brightness panel and are typically available for $350 to $400. Meanwhile, the 271QP X24 and 273QP X24 both use the full-brightness 240Hz panel.
That's nowhere near enough differentiation in the naming. If anything, the model numbers make the limited-brightness versions sound newer or higher-end, with the 274QP appearing to sit above the 273QP. So if you're shopping for an MSI QD-OLED, you'll need to pay very close attention to the exact model number. A single digit in the middle of the product name can determine which panel you're actually getting.
These aren't all of the budget 1440p QD-OLEDs currently on the market. As mentioned, there are several minor variants of the products we're testing here, along with a handful of models we haven't been able to get our hands on yet. We'll continue to test more monitors in this category, but these 11 models provide a good starting point for understanding the current budget QD-OLED landscape.
QD-OLED Similarities: Panel Coating and Subpixel Layout
While there are three panel variants used across these budget QD-OLED monitors, all of them use the same generation of QD-OLED technology and share the same baseline capabilities. The panel structure, layout, per-pixel control, and deep-black performance are effectively identical across all 11 monitors in this round-up.
That means characteristics such as black depth, screen coating, and subpixel layout are the same regardless of which variant you buy.
The screen coating on all 11 models is the same glossy QD-OLED finish we've seen for several years now. Its main strengths are a grain-free appearance that delivers excellent clarity, along with very good reflection handling. Because it's glossy, there is still some mirror-like reflectivity, but direct reflections are generally more subdued than on many other glossy displays. If you're using the monitor in an environment where light sources aren't directly hitting the screen, it's a great coating that produces a vibrant, clear image.
The main weakness is ambient-light reflectivity. In moderately to brightly lit environments, QD-OLED panels reflect ambient light in a way that raises black levels and gives the screen a slight reddish-purple tint. Under these conditions, blacks can appear gray rather than properly black, reducing one of OLED's biggest advantages.
You can mitigate this by positioning light sources so they don't hit the display directly, but that won't be practical for everyone. Ultimately, it's a limitation of this type of panel, and one reason QD-OLED monitors are best suited to darker rooms where the strengths of the technology can really shine.
Text rendering is also identical across all of these budget 1440p QD-OLEDs because they use the same triangular RGB subpixel layout. Since this isn't a traditional RGB stripe, it isn't fully compatible with modern subpixel font-rendering techniques.
As a result, text quality isn't as good as on monitors that use a conventional RGB stripe, such as most LCDs. With the triangular RGB layout, you may notice faint pink and green fringing around the top and bottom edges of text, which reduces overall clarity and can be a downgrade if you're coming from an LCD.
Text Rendering Quality
That said, we've heard from plenty of users who barely notice the issue, so how distracting it is will depend on your sensitivity to these artifacts and how much time you spend reading text. The subpixel layout has essentially no impact when watching video or playing games, where these displays look excellent.
Brightness: SDR and HDR
Brightness is where the different panel variants start to separate more clearly, which makes sense given that some are designed with limited brightness while others offer the full capabilities of QD-OLED. This affects both SDR and HDR performance, starting with SDR.
All of the full-brightness monitors are capable of around 250 nits in full-screen white SDR content, with no meaningful difference between them. The limited-brightness models, meanwhile, typically achieve around 190 to 200 nits. There's slightly more variation within this lower-brightness group. For example, we measured the Gigabyte GO27Q24A at around 8% brighter than the Dell AW2726DM, but broadly speaking these are 200-nit displays.
That means the full-brightness models are ultimately capable of around 25% higher SDR brightness.
But does that actually matter? It depends on your use case.
We generally find 200 nits sufficient for indoor use in a moderately lit or darker room, particularly where glare isn't an issue. In those conditions, we'd often turn down a 250-nit monitor anyway for a more comfortable viewing experience.
But if you use your monitor in a brighter room, deal with significant glare, need extra brightness to overcome reflections, or simply prefer running your display at high brightness levels, 200 nits may not be enough. In that situation, opting for a full-brightness QD-OLED makes much more sense.
Minimum brightness is very good across the board. The highest minimum we measured was around 30 nits, which is already quite low and should be perfectly usable in dark environments. A few monitors can get much dimmer, particularly the Asus and AOC models, although we're not sure how practical it would be to actually use one at around 10 nits.
HDR Is Where the Gap Gets Much Larger
The difference between the limited- and full-brightness panels becomes much more pronounced in HDR. Starting again with full-screen brightness, performance is broadly similar to what we saw in SDR. The full-brightness models sit between roughly 250 and 270 nits, while the limited-brightness models range from around 186 to 216 nits. The AOC and Dell models post particularly low results here compared with the rest of the group.
The gap narrows somewhat with a 10% window, although the full-brightness models still hold an advantage. Most of them deliver between 455 and 485 nits, a spread of only around 7% from the lowest to highest result.
The limited-brightness models fall between roughly 380 and 435 nits. In the worst cases, that's up to 20% dimmer than the full-brightness models, although some get surprisingly close. The Gigabyte GO27Q24A, for example, trails the higher-tier models by only around 20 nits.
The biggest difference appears in peak brightness, represented by our 2% window test. All six full-brightness monitors we tested are capable of exceeding 1,000 nits. None of the limited-brightness models reaches even 450 nits.
That's a massive difference. In the best cases, the full-brightness models can deliver more than twice the peak luminance of the limited variants. Interestingly, even when the full-brightness models are switched into their "True Black" modes, which typically reduce peak brightness in exchange for improved accuracy, they still slightly outperform the limited-brightness models. So while the size of the advantage varies depending on the content and window size, the full-brightness models are consistently brighter.
For the written version of this round-up, we've deliberately skipped some of the deeper testing around HDR mode configurations, HDR and SDR calibration, and color accuracy to keep the article focused on the information most relevant to a buying decision. Those results are covered in detail in the video for readers who want to dig further into the data.
Ports and Features
Connectivity is fairly basic on most of these monitors. The AOC Q27G40ZDF has the weakest port selection, with just one DisplayPort input, one HDMI port limited to HDMI 2.0 speeds, and no USB ports at all. The Dell AW2726DM is also fairly lackluster, although it at least provides two HDMI 2.0 ports.
Every other model offers HDMI 2.1 alongside a DisplayPort 1.4 connection.
| Monitor | DisplayPort | HDMI | USB-C | USB Hub | USB Hub Speed | KVM Switch | Power Supply | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Acer Predator X27U X1 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | No | No | No | No | External Brick | 
| AOC Q27G40ZDF | 1x 1.4 DSC | 1x 2.0 18 Gbps | No | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMES | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes (service only) | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Dell Alienware AW2725D | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD (no DP-Alt) | Yes, 2 Port | 5 Gbps | No | Internal | 
| Dell Alienware AW2726DM | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.0 18 Gbps | No | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Gigabyte GO27Q24A | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | No | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Gigabyte MO27Q2 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 18W PD, DP-Alt | Yes, 2 Port | 5 Gbps | Yes | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 271QP X28 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD, DP-Alt | No | No | No | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 271QPX E2 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD, DP-Alt | No | No | No | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 272QP X24 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 40 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD, DP-Alt | No | No | No | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 273QP X24 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | No | No | No | No | External Brick | 
Several monitors also include USB-C, although the implementation varies. On the Dell AW2725D, USB-C does not function as a display input, while on the Asus XG27AQDMES it is reserved for service use.
Three of the MSI models support DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C with 15W of power delivery, although they don't include additional USB ports. Only two monitors offer a proper USB hub: the Dell AW2725D and Gigabyte MO27Q2. Of those, only the Gigabyte also includes KVM functionality and USB-C with DP Alt Mode.
From a connectivity standpoint, the MO27Q2 clearly has the strongest port selection of the group, although most of the other models still provide a basic but sufficient set of inputs.
Useful OSD Features
Each monitor includes additional features accessible through the OSD, and most provide the usual mix of color controls and gaming features such as crosshairs and FPS counters. Rather than going through every common setting, we'll focus on the more notable differences we found during testing.
The Asus XG27AQDMES is the only model here with a proximity sensor that can automatically switch off the OLED panel when you leave your desk. We've seen this feature implemented across several Asus OLED monitors, and we're pleased to see it make its way to the more affordable AQDMES as well. It works well and is a useful complement to the other OLED care features.
Several displays also include black frame insertion, which can operate at 120Hz to provide motion clarity closer to 240Hz. As we've mentioned in previous reviews, however, this is a fairly inflexible feature because it requires disabling variable refresh rate support. The monitors that include this are the MSI 271QP X28 and 272QP X24 (labeled MPRT), the Asus XG27AQDMES (labeled ELMB) and the Gigabyte GO27Q24A (labeled Ultra Clear).
Two models also include an Anti-Flicker feature: the Asus XG27AQDMES and Gigabyte GO27Q24A. This lets you raise the minimum refresh rate used during variable refresh operation, which can help reduce flicker when frame rates fluctuate heavily. It's a moderately useful feature and we're glad to see it included, even if it's not a game changer.
Acer's HDR Switching Is a Pain
On a more negative note, the Acer Predator X27U X1 handles switching between SDR and HDR very poorly. There is an "Auto" HDR mode, but it isn't actually automatic. Selecting this option keeps the monitor in its HDR configuration even when HDR is disabled in the operating system, which can lead to incorrect-looking colors.
For the best experience, you need to manually change OSD settings depending on whether you're using SDR or HDR, which is unnecessarily cumbersome. The monitor also has particularly annoying OLED panel-cleaning warnings compared with the other models. They appear frequently and require user interaction before disappearing.
OLED Care and Burn-In Warranties
Each display includes a different set of OLED care controls for features such as automatic dimming, edge dimming, pixel shifting, and related protections. Having some control over these features is useful, particularly if you find certain dimming behaviors distracting or overly aggressive.
MSI does the best job here, offering both the ability to disable some OLED care functions and adjust others, including the delay before dimming activates and the strength of the dimming effect. The AOC also provides some customization for individual OLED care features, although not to the same extent as the MSI models.
Asus offers a good range of options as well, though most are simple on/off toggles. Gigabyte's implementation is similar, but with slightly fewer controls. Acer provides only a handful of OLED care settings, while Dell offers no user control over these features at all, making its monitors the weakest in this area.
As for burn-in, all of these monitors use fundamentally similar panel hardware, so the underlying risk of permanent image retention should be broadly comparable. Actual behavior will still depend on usage patterns and which OLED care features are enabled, but at the hardware level these panels use the same type of emissive technology.
Based on publicly available warranty information, all six brands represented in this round-up offer a three-year burn-in warranty for these displays, which has effectively become the industry standard.
Monitor Design and Build Quality
We're not going to spend too much time on aesthetics because monitor design is ultimately subjective. You may simply prefer the look of one model over another, and that's perfectly reasonable. However, there are some meaningful differences in ergonomics, stand design, build quality, and general usability.
The AOC Q27G40ZDF, along with its closely related variants, uses a fixed-height stand. It's the only monitor in this round-up that doesn't offer height adjustment. That's a significant downside, especially because the AOC isn't substantially cheaper than many competing models that do provide a fully adjustable stand. Build quality is also fairly basic, and the monitor lacks a directional joystick for navigating the OSD. Instead, menu navigation is more cumbersome than it needs to be.
Every other monitor here includes a directional control, so from an ergonomic and usability perspective, the AOC is the weakest of the group.
The Dell AW2726DM is also relatively basic, although it does include height adjustment.
MSI's models are broadly similar to one another in both styling and build quality. They're perfectly acceptable overall, without doing anything particularly noteworthy.
The Acer Predator X27U X1 uses a wide V-shaped stand base. Personally, we don't think this works as well as the smaller, flatter bases used by many of the competing models because it occupies noticeably more desk space.
Gigabyte's design is one of our favorites in this group, and it's used across both the M-series and G-series models with only minor variations. You get a height-adjustable stand, a directional joystick for the OSD, and a very nice metal stand base with a thin metal pillar. Build quality is excellent for a budget-oriented product.
The Asus XG27AQDMES is also particularly well built, with a compact metal stand base and above-average overall construction. Lastly, the Dell AW2725D is another strong design. Although most of its external surfaces are plastic, the quality and finish of that plastic are noticeably better than on many of the other monitors in this round-up.
Picking Winners: The Best Options
As we've emphasized throughout this article, the most important thing to understand is that there are two versions of the 240Hz 1440p QD-OLED panel: one with the usual 1,000-nit peak brightness capability, and another limited to around 400 nits. It's not always obvious which panel a monitor is using, but this is one of the biggest differences between the options on the market today.
The 1,000-nit panel is simply better. Everything the limited-brightness 400-nit panel can do, the full-brightness version can also do, while adding around 25% higher SDR brightness and a huge increase in peak HDR output. In our view, the full-brightness panel is also the only one of the two that delivers a genuinely convincing HDR experience. So if two monitors cost roughly the same and one uses the full-brightness panel while the other doesn't, the choice is obvious.
How Much Should You Pay?
The going rate for a 27-inch 1440p limited-brightness QD-OLED is around $350. Multiple models are regularly available at that price, and we wouldn't pay more than $350 for this panel regardless of the official MSRP. Closer to $300 is even better, and we've seen some models approach that level over the last few months.
Given the HDR performance advantage, we'd be comfortable paying around 25% more for a full-brightness model. Around $400 is an excellent deal, while $450 is still reasonable.
The good news is that most of the monitors covered here have already been available within those price ranges. The 280Hz Alienware AW2725D, for example, recently dropped to $400. The MSI 271QP X28 is regularly available for around $450, while most of the 240Hz limited-brightness models sell for $350 or less.
The Best Budget QD-OLED Options
It's encouraging that most of these 1440p QD-OLED monitors are genuinely good. There isn't a single model in this round-up that we'd avoid entirely because of a major flaw. Regional pricing also varies significantly, so any of them could make sense if heavily discounted.
If you're on a tighter budget and simply want the cheapest good-value QD-OLED, this is where the limited-brightness models make the most sense. They still provide a high refresh rate, excellent motion clarity, very good image quality, and the outstanding contrast you'd expect from OLED.
We tested five models in this category and ended up with two clear standouts. The Gigabyte GO27Q24A is our preferred option, with better HDR and SDR calibration, a higher-quality design, and a stronger feature set than the rest of the group. The MSI 272QP X24 is a close second and also a strong choice at the right price.
Our Top Overall Pick: Dell Alienware AW2725D
The Dell Alienware AW2725D is our top overall pick. It delivers well-balanced performance across both SDR and HDR, generally strong calibration, a higher 280Hz refresh rate, and a very good physical design. There are a few weaknesses. Dell provides no customization for its OLED care features, and the monitor lacks a boosted-brightness HDR mode. But across the complete package, we think the AW2725D strikes the best balance of the models tested here.
At its original $550 MSRP, it isn't especially compelling today. At around $400 on sale, however, it becomes a much stronger proposition. We've already seen it reach that price, and with the holiday shopping period approaching, we'd expect similar discounts to appear again.
As for the other full-brightness options, the Acer Predator X27U X1 loses points because of its awkward SDR-to-HDR switching. The Gigabyte MO27Q2 lacks a proper "Peak" HDR mode and is becoming difficult to find, having largely been replaced by the newer MO27Q2A.
The MSI 271QPX E2 has the weakest calibration among the full-brightness models and doesn't offer enough standout features to compensate. We also weren't overly impressed with the MSI 271QP X28. Its 280Hz refresh rate is a plus, but it suffers from noticeable black crush in SDR, although HDR performance is better and it supports all three major HDR configurations.
The MSI model we prefer is actually the 273QP X24, but it has some HDR saturation issues and has been discontinued in several markets, making it difficult to recommend broadly.

articles.title: The iPad Mini is slightly cheaper again during Prime Day
articles.text:
Apple bumped up prices on several of its devices in June, and we haven’t seen a good discount on the iPad Mini since. Just ahead of Amazon’s October Prime Big Deals Days, however, both Wi-Fi only and cellular-connected models are $100 off. The Wi-Fi version with 128GB of storage is currently $499, the 256GB model is $599, and the cellular model with 128GB of storage is $649.
The iPad Mini is slightly cheaper again during Prime Day
With a $100 discount, the Apple iPad Mini is temporarily back to its pre-RAMageddon price.
This base configuration of this tablet often sold for around $400 throughout 2025, so we get it if $500 for a tablet from late 2024 is still too much. But it’s the best price since late June, and if there’s a new version coming out later this year, it might be significantly more expensive.
iPad Mini (2024)
The seventh-gen iPad Mini comes with Apple’s A17 Pro chip and support for Apple Intelligence. It’s also compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and offers faster Wi-Fi and USB-C speeds. Read our review.
We reviewed this version of the iPad Mini when it launched in 2024, and while we appreciated the processor upgrade and Apple Intelligence features, it felt lacking in some of the quality-of-life improvements found in the larger iPads that launched around the same time.

articles.title: Do voto ao resultado: entenda o caminho dos dados após o fim da votação
articles.text:
Quando a votação termina, o trabalho da Justiça Eleitoral está longe de acabar. Depois que a última pessoa autorizada a votar deixa a cabine, os dados registrados na urna eletrônica passam por uma sequência de procedimentos até serem incorporados à totalização dos resultados.
Nas Eleições 2026, o 1º turno está sendo realizado neste domingo (4). A votação começou às 8h e vai até as 17h, no horário de Brasília, mas quem estiver na fila às 17h ainda terá direito de votar. A seção eleitoral só é encerrada depois que todos os eleitores que receberam senha terminam a votação.
O que acontece quando a votação termina?
- Concluída a votação, a própria urna eletrônica apura os votos registrados naquela seção e imprime o Boletim de Urna (BU). O documento apresenta o resultado da seção, incluindo os votos de cada candidatura e legenda e o número de eleitores que compareceram;
- São impressas obrigatoriamente cinco vias do BU. Uma delas é afixada na porta da sala onde funcionou a seção eleitoral;
- Na sequência, o presidente da mesa retira da urna a chamada mídia de resultado, um dispositivo removível que armazena os dados da votação. Ela é assinada e lacrada antes de ser encaminhada para a transmissão;
- A mídia contém o Boletim de Urna em formato digital, com os votos atribuídos a cada candidatura e legenda, sem qualquer relação entre o eleitor e o voto. Também estão no arquivo informações sobre a seção e a urna que produziram o BU, além do número de eleitores que compareceram e votaram.
Como os dados chegam ao TSE?
A urna eletrônica não possui conexão com a internet nem com outras redes de dados. Por isso, os arquivos são transmitidos por uma rede de comunicação utilizada especificamente para essa finalidade. Em locais de difícil acesso, a Justiça Eleitoral adota procedimentos próprios para o envio das informações.
A forma de recolhimento das mídias e de transmissão dos dados é definida pela juíza ou pelo juiz responsável por cada zona eleitoral. Elas podem ser levadas à sede da zona eleitoral, encaminhadas a um ponto de transmissão ou entregues diretamente a um servidor do tribunal ou profissional de apoio responsável pela transmissão, quando o procedimento ocorre no próprio local de votação.
Quando a transmissão ocorre a partir do cartório eleitoral, é utilizado o Sistema Transportador, que opera por uma rede criptografada. Já em pontos de transmissão instalados fora das sedes dos cartórios, a Justiça Eleitoral utiliza o JE-Connect.
O sistema JE-Connect foi desenvolvido pela própria Justiça Eleitoral e permite acelerar a totalização porque elimina a necessidade de transportar as mídias de resultado até os cartórios para realizar a transmissão. A tecnologia atualmente está presente em todos os estados brasileiros.
Nos pontos de transmissão, os arquivos criptografados das mídias de resultado são enviados por computadores conectados a uma rede privada virtual (VPN, na sigla em inglês). Os dados já saem criptografados da urna e recebem nova camada de criptografia durante o processo.
O que acontece com os dados depois da transmissão?
Antes que os resultados sejam incorporados à totalização, os sistemas da Justiça Eleitoral verificam a autenticidade e a integridade dos arquivos.
Uma dessas etapas envolve a conferência da assinatura digital, que confirma que o resultado foi produzido pela urna eletrônica cadastrada para aquela seção. Depois das verificações, os resultados são incorporados à totalização.
A totalização é realizada pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), em Brasília (DF). O tribunal disponibiliza em seu portal os Boletins de Urna enviados para totalização e as tabelas de correspondências realizadas durante o período em que recebe os dados.
Após a totalização final, os BUs são publicados e podem ser comparados com os boletins gerados pelas urnas de cada seção eleitoral. A conferência pode ser feita pelo documento impresso ou pela leitura do QR Code presente nele, por meio do aplicativo Boletim na Mão.
O resultado final das Eleições 2026 será divulgado nos portais do TSE e dos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais (TREs), além do aplicativo Resultados.
Leia mais:
- Starlink será usada pelo TSE em locais remotos nas eleições 2026
- STF amplia acesso gratuito a serviços do TSE e sites de checagem nas eleições
- Eleições 2026: buscas no Google sobre multa eleitoral e venda de bebidas disparam
Como os votos são armazenados na urna?
Além dos dados gravados na mídia de resultado, os votos são registrados no Registro Digital do Voto (RDV). Trata-se de uma tabela digital na qual os votos são armazenados de maneira aleatória, sem revelar a ordem em que as pessoas votaram.
O mecanismo funciona de maneira semelhante a uma urna de lona, na qual as cédulas de papel ficam embaralhadas. O RDV utiliza ferramentas de segurança da informação, como criptografia, assinatura digital e hash.
O registro digital também permite uma recontagem automatizada dos votos. Partidos políticos e coligações podem obter cópias dos arquivos de RDV das urnas que considerarem necessárias e desenvolver aplicativos próprios para comparar a apuração oficial com aquela produzida por seus sistemas.
Como funciona a totalização?
A etapa de totalização não consiste simplesmente em somar todos os votos da mesma maneira. O processo considera as regras específicas dos sistemas majoritário e proporcional.
No sistema majoritário, utilizado nas eleições para presidente, governador e senador, é considerada a candidatura ou chapa que obtiver a maior quantidade de votos válidos, conforme as regras de cada cargo.
Já no sistema proporcional, utilizado para deputado federal, deputado estadual ou distrital, a distribuição das vagas considera os votos recebidos pelas candidaturas e aqueles destinados aos partidos e às federações.
Também existem regras específicas para votos de candidaturas que ainda tenham pendências relacionadas ao registro. Na eleição majoritária, por exemplo, a validade definitiva dos votos de uma chapa cujo registro esteja sob recurso ou ainda não tenha sido analisado depende da decisão final que defira o registro.
Na eleição proporcional, votos de candidaturas cujo registro esteja deferido, ainda seja objeto de recurso ou não tenha sido analisado podem ser considerados válidos. Caso o registro seja posteriormente indeferido ou cancelado nas situações previstas, os votos passam a ser contabilizados para o partido pelo qual a candidatura concorreu.
Quem proclama os eleitos?
Depois da totalização, entra em cena outra etapa: a proclamação dos resultados.
Nos estados e no Distrito Federal, cabe aos TREs proclamar os eleitos para governador e vice-governador, senador e respectivos suplentes, além de deputados federais, distritais e estaduais e seus suplentes. No caso da Presidência da República, a responsabilidade pela proclamação dos eleitos é do TSE.
Nas eleições majoritárias, são proclamadas as chapas com a maior votação válida, seguindo as regras específicas para situações que envolvam votos anulados ainda sob análise judicial. Já nas eleições proporcionais, a distribuição das vagas considera os votos válidos atribuídos a candidatos e legendas, excluindo os votos em branco e nulos.
A legislação também prevê que, se uma votação for definitivamente anulada e os votos anulados representarem mais de 50% dos votos atribuídos a candidatos e legendas, uma nova eleição deverá ser marcada.
E depois da proclamação?
A última etapa é a diplomação. Ela confirma o resultado das urnas e formaliza a condição de eleito ou suplente.
Governadores, senadores e deputados recebem os diplomas dos respectivos TREs. Já os diplomas de presidente e vice-presidente da República são emitidos pelo TSE.
O documento informa o nome da pessoa eleita, o partido, a federação ou coligação e o cargo conquistado ou a condição de suplente. Quando houver registro, o nome social é utilizado.
Candidatos com registro indeferido não podem ser diplomados, mesmo que ainda estejam recorrendo da decisão. A expedição do diploma pode ser contestada em até três dias após o prazo final de diplomação, enquanto o mandato pode ser questionado na Justiça Eleitoral em até 15 dias após a diplomação, desde que a ação seja acompanhada de provas de abuso do poder econômico, corrupção ou fraude.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Cette barre de son LG 7.1.3 avec enceintes arrière et compatible Dolby Atmos/DTX:X ne dépasse pas les 400 € — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est un fait : même les téléviseurs les plus haut de gamme peinent à délivrer un son vraiment puissant, à la hauteur de leurs performances d’image. Une barre de son devient donc vite indispensable pour profiter d’une expérience plus immersive. C’est justement ce qu’offre la LG S90TR, une barre de son accompagnée d’enceintes arrière sans fil et d’un caisson de basses. Configurée en 7.1.3 et compatible Dolby Atmos, elle devrait convenir aux amateurs de films, de séries et de jeux vidéo. Et la bonne nouvelle, c’est que son prix ne dépasse pas les 400 euros.
Les points forts de la LG S90TR
- Une barre de son avec un caisson de basses et deux enceintes surround
- Un système 7.1.3 canaux
- La spatialisation Dolby Atmos/DTS:X
Affichée à plus de 600 euros sur d’autres sites, la barre de son LG S90TR (avec son caisson de basses et ses enceintes arrière) est aujourd’hui proposée à 399,98 euros par Électro Dépôt.
Immersion assurée
La LG S90TR est tout d’abord une barre de son assez imposante (1 250 x 63 x 135 mm) : mieux vaut donc l’associer à un grand téléviseur, pour conserver une installation équilibrée. Heureusement, son caisson de basses ainsi que ses enceintes arrière se connectent sans fil à la barre de son, ce qui évite de devoir tirer des câbles à travers le salon.
Par ailleurs, ce système, dont la puissance atteint 670 W, compte en tout 10 haut-parleurs, répartis dans une configuration 7.1.3 canaux. Cinq sont intégrés à la barre, dont trois orientés vers le plafond pour élargir la scène sonore, tandis que les enceintes surround en accueillent chacune deux. Le dernier haut-parleur, dédié aux basses, se trouve dans le caisson.
Le tout est compatible Dolby Atmos et DTS:X. Bref, vous avez de quoi profiter d’un véritable son surround physique, grâce notamment aux enceintes satellites, que vous pouvez placer juste derrière vous, et aux haut-parleurs verticaux intégrés dans la barre. De quoi créer une bulle sonore bien immersive, avec des effets qui semblent provenir de différentes directions.
D’autres fonctionnalités pour améliorer l’expérience
La barre de son dispose également de plusieurs fonctionnalités intelligentes qui peuvent améliorer l’expérience sonore. Par exemple, la fonction AI Room Calibration Pro se charge d’analyser la pièce dans laquelle la barre de son se trouve pour corriger toute distorsion sonore. La technologie WOW Orchestra, elle, synchronise le son de la barre avec celui d’un téléviseur LG pour enrichir la scène sonore. Enfin, l’AI Sound Pro détecte le type de contenu visionné et applique l’égaliseur le plus adapté.
Pour finir, côté connectivité, la barre de son se montre assez polyvalente avec la prise en charge de Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Google Cast, AirPlay 2 ainsi que le Wi-Fi et le Bluetooth 5.1. Elle est aussi compatible Google Home et Alexa. Côté connectique, c’est du classique avec une entrée HDMI, une sortie HDMI eARC, une entrée optique et un port USB. La barre prend d’ailleurs en charge le VRR et l’ALLM, ce qui permet de conserver ces fonctions gaming lorsqu’une console est branchée sur la barre.
Si vous souhaitez découvrir d’autres modèles que nous recommandons, nous vous invitons dès maintenant à consulter notre guide des meilleures barres de son du moment.

articles.title: Agents have made CI the bottleneck. Faster pipelines are the wrong fix.
articles.text:
Agents have made CI the bottleneck. Faster pipelines are the wrong fix.
Three posts landed in September that I think engineering leaders should read together.
Anthropic’s engineering team wrote that their continuous integration (CI) job volume grew 25x in six months. Their engineers now ship about 8x as much code per quarter as they did from 2021 to 2025. The fix they shipped was test impact analysis: run only the tests a change could affect.
A week later, Linear published a post titled AI coding has made CI a bottleneck. Their test suite has nearly quadrupled since January, and agents now write most of their tests. They reworked the pipeline end to end to keep up.
Then Depot’s CEO wrote that CI is changing, and that the future is “giving agents a way to validate code and maintain trust as they work.”
Anthropic and Linear do not sell CI tooling. They are reporting what happened to their own pipelines, which is what makes it worth paying attention to. Here is my read: all three are right about the problem, and two of them are fixing the wrong layer.
How CI became the bottleneck
For twenty years, CI was sized for human output. A developer opened a few pull requests (PRs) a week, and the pipeline ran after each one. If it took 20 minutes, nobody cared much, because the developer was already on the next task.
Agents broke that arithmetic in two ways. First, volume. When one engineer runs several agents in parallel, PR count goes up by a multiple, not a percentage. Anthropic’s 25x number is not an outlier. Blacksmith, which sells CI runners, says the number of CI jobs it runs has grown between 5% and 10% week over week.
The agent is fast, and the loop around it is slow.
Second, placement. CI runs after the PR exists. An agent that writes code, opens a PR, and waits 20 minutes for a red check has lost its working context by the time the result comes back. Every failure costs a full round trip. The agent is fast, and the loop around it is slow.
So the industry did the obvious thing and made CI faster. Faster runners, smarter test selection, bigger caches, pipelines that agents can call before commit. All of it helps, and all of it is necessary. All of it also leaves one assumption untouched: that what you’re verifying is a repository.
What a green pipeline does not tell you
For a standalone application, a repository is the system. Run the tests, and you know most of what you need to know.
For a cloud-native system, a repository is one service out of forty. The tests in that repo exercise that service, and they mock everything else. A change can pass every unit test, pass CI in record time, pass a sandbox built from the branch, and still break the first real request that crosses a service boundary.
The failures that hurt in distributed systems live in the seams. A field renamed in a response that a downstream consumer still reads. A timeout tightened in one service that cascades into retries somewhere else. A schema change that works against the test fixture and locks a table in staging. A new endpoint that behaves correctly when the test harness calls it and incorrectly when the service that depends on it calls it.
Nothing in the CI pipeline, fast or slow, sees any of that. It cannot, because it is looking at a repo.
This is why I think the September posts are a symptom, not a diagnosis. CI got slow because verification moved from a human gate to an automated one without anyone asking what the automated gate checks. Making the gate faster does not change what it checks.
Faster code, same verification, more breakage. That is the gap.
DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) found something that should worry you: higher AI adoption is associated with increases in both software delivery throughput and software delivery instability. Faster code, same verification, more breakage. That is the gap.
The verification loop has to move
Cursor made a point in February that is only becoming more relevant. Their agents run in cloud sandboxes, each with its own virtual machine, and more than 30% of the PRs Cursor merges now come from agents working that way. Their stated reason: “Without the ability to use the software they are creating, agents hit a ceiling.”
That is the right instinct. The agent has to run the code, not only write it. Every serious coding agent now does some version of this. GitHub’s Copilot cloud agent runs tests in an ephemeral environment powered by GitHub Actions. Codex runs a setup script and resumes cached containers. Devin boots from environment blueprints. Greptile’s TREX runs the branch and attaches logs and screenshots to the PR.
But look at what each of those sandboxes contains: the repo, the branch, and whatever the setup script could install. None of them include the other 39 services, the real message queue, or the database with production-shaped data.
So the loop closes, but it closes around the wrong thing.
So the loop closes, but it closes around the wrong thing. The agent verifies its change against a copy of its own code. Then the change goes to CI, which verifies it against the same copy, faster. Then it merges into staging, and that is the first moment anything checks whether it works with the rest of the system.
For distributed systems, verification before the PR has to be against the system, not the repo. That is the shift. It is not faster feedback on the same question. It is a different question, asked earlier.
Why this looks expensive and is not
The reflexive objection is cost. If every agent needs the whole system to verify against, and one engineer is running five agents, you need five staging environments per engineer. Nobody can afford that, and nobody should try.
The answer is the same one the industry used for compute two decades ago. You do not give every workload its own machine. You multiplex.
A single Kubernetes cluster can run one shared stable version of every service and host thousands of lightweight test environments on top of it. Each test environment deploys only the changed service. Requests tagged for that environment pass through the modified service, and every other hop resolves to the shared stable versions. The modified service talks to real dependencies, and those dependencies do not know anything changed.
A test environment costs roughly the price of one pod, and it comes up in seconds. Fifty agents working in parallel share one stable environment instead of cloning it fifty times. That is what makes system-level verification inside the agent loop affordable in the first place.
Agents need governed verification, not only environments
Cheap, fast environments are not the whole answer. An agent also needs a structured way to use them: send this request, capture that log, assert this contract held, report the result. Left to improvise, each agent invents its own checks, and no two runs are comparable.
The model that works is one where the platform team writes those steps once, as a sequence of approved actions that exercises a change against the live system and records what happened. Agents invoke them through the skills and hooks that Claude Code, Cursor, and similar tools already support, so verification runs as part of the loop rather than after it. The governance matters as much as the steps, because platform teams need to know an agent cannot do something unsafe in a shared cluster.
The output matters too. A record showing which requests were sent, which services were touched, and which contracts were held is an artifact the next layer can read. Review tools and merge gates can see that a change was exercised against live services before a human looks at it, and CI becomes a confirmation step instead of the first place cross-service breakage shows up.
Verification belongs inside the agent’s loop
I expect the CI vendors to keep getting faster, and I expect coding agents to keep getting better at running code in sandboxes. Both are good for everyone, and neither closes the gap between a repo and a system. The teams that come out ahead will stop asking how fast the pipeline can confirm that a repo still passes its own tests and start asking how early an agent can prove that a change works with everything around it. That question gets answered in one place: inside the agent’s loop, against the real system, before the PR. We built Signadot to make that check cheap enough to run on every change, with the governed.

articles.title: The forgotten Chromebook that started it all
articles.text:
Google didn’t even call the first Chromebook a “Chromebook.” The Cr-48 had no interesting design and no bright logos – it wasn’t even designed to be a product you could buy. Instead, it was a portal to a big new idea about computers.
The forgotten Chromebook that started it all
On Version History: Marques Brownlee and Nilay Patel relive the release of the Cr-48, Google’s prototype laptop.
In this week’s episode of Version History, The Verge’s Nilay Patel and MKBHD’s Marques Brownlee join David Pierce to help explain the history of ChromeOS and Chromebooks, and discuss whether Google’s approach to computer hardware was the right one.
This has been an exciting season of Version History, as we’ve been exploring the most iconic school tech. Last week’s episode explored Nicholas Negroponte’s One Laptop Per Child XO-1 and his goals for a global distribution. We’ve also talked to the lead game designer of The Oregon Trail and learned why everyone had to own a TI graphing calculator. If you missed these episodes, check out them out below:

articles.title: Google vai limitar acesso a modelos do Gemini para usuários gratuitos e AI Plus
articles.text:
O Google vai mudar, a partir de 9 de outubro, quais modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) ficam disponíveis para usuários do Gemini. A alteração afetará tanto pessoas que utilizam o serviço gratuitamente quanto assinantes do plano Google AI Plus.
Segundo informações divulgadas pelo 9to5Google com base em documento de suporte atualizado pelo Google, usuários sem assinatura de um plano de IA perderão o acesso aos modelos Gemini 3.6 Flash e Gemini 3.1 Pro. Eles ficarão limitados ao Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.
A mudança ocorre depois de o Google alterar, em maio, a forma de contabilizar o uso do Gemini com base na quantidade de recursos computacionais utilizados. Agora, a empresa também passará a diferenciar os modelos disponíveis de acordo com o plano contratado.
O que muda para cada plano
- Quem utiliza o Gemini sem um plano pago continuará tendo acesso ao Flash-Lite, mas perderá os modelos Flash e Pro;
- Para os assinantes do Google AI Plus, que pagam US$ 4,99 por mês (cerca de R$ 27), o Gemini continuará oferecendo Flash-Lite e Flash, mas o modelo Pro deixará de estar disponível;
- O 9to5Google afirma que esses usuários receberão um e-mail informando quando a alteração será aplicada;
- Já os assinantes dos planos AI Pro e AI Ultra não terão redução no acesso aos modelos. Ambos continuarão com Flash-Lite, Flash e Pro.
Confira, abaixo, uma tabela que clarifica o tema:
| Plano | Flash-Lite | Flash | Pro | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Sem plano | ✓ | — | — | 
| AI Plus | ✓ | ✓ | — | 
| AI Pro | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 
| AI Ultra | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 
Leia mais:
- Gemini agora atende o telefone por você — e você pode assumir a qualquer momento
- Gemini ganha rosto: nova inteligência artificial do Google fala, reage e sincroniza os lábios em tempo real
- Adobe reúne mais de 80 ferramentas no Claude e leva Photoshop, Lightroom e Firefly ao Gemini
AI Pro ganha recurso de raciocínio avançado
Enquanto usuários gratuitos e do AI Plus perderão acesso a modelos, o plano AI Pro receberá novo recurso.
Assinantes do plano de US$ 19,99 por mês (cerca de R$ 109) passarão a ter acesso ao Deep Think, opção descrita pelo Google como voltada ao “raciocínio paralelo máximo”.
Até agora, o recurso estava disponível apenas para assinantes do AI Ultra, cujos planos custam US$ 99,99 e US$ 199,99 por mês (cerca de R$ 544 e R$ 1.087).
Gemini terá novos níveis de raciocínio
Outra mudança prevista para outubro é a inclusão de três níveis de esforço para os modelos disponíveis no aplicativo: baixo, médio e alto.
A ideia é permitir que o usuário escolha quanto esforço o Gemini deve empregar para resolver uma tarefa. De acordo com a descrição citada pelo 9to5Google, níveis mais altos podem aumentar a capacidade do modelo de realizar tarefas e produzir respostas mais detalhadas, mas também consumirão mais do limite de uso.
Atualmente, o Gemini oferece a opção de “Extended thinking”, voltada à resolução de problemas complexos. Os novos níveis devem aproximar o funcionamento do aplicativo das opções já disponíveis no Google AI Studio e no Antigravity.
E o Gemini 4 Argon?
Ainda não está definido onde o Gemini 4 Argon, novo modelo avançado do Google, ficará dentro dessa estrutura de planos.
O Google anunciou que o modelo será disponibilizado inicialmente para assinantes do AI Ultra, mas ainda não informou se o Argon será classificado como um modelo Pro ou se fará parte de uma nova categoria acima desse nível.
O próprio Google também mantém páginas de suporte que descrevem limites de uso e disponibilidade de modelos como sujeitos a mudanças, dependendo de fatores, como capacidade do sistema e experimentos.
Na prática, a partir de 9 de outubro, a principal mudança para quem usa o Gemini sem pagar será a perda de acesso aos modelos Flash e Pro, enquanto assinantes do AI Plus também deixarão de contar com o Pro. Os planos superiores, por outro lado, manterão o acesso aos três modelos e ganharão novos recursos de raciocínio.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.
